findings: Chapter 2 of the 3rd edition introduces the Boolean values True and False, the six comparison operators, the Boolean operators and, or and not, how comparison and Boolean operators mix, the components of flow control - conditions and blocks - and the if, else and elif statements, with two short programs.

The reference documentation makes precise what the chapter leaves informal: and and or return one of their operands rather than a Boolean - x and y returns x if x is false - and evaluate the second operand only when needed; comparisons chain, so x < y <= z means x < y and y <= z; many values besides False count as false, including None, zero of any numeric type and empty sequences; the conditional expression x if C else y chooses a value in one line; and PEP 8 advises against comparing Boolean values to True or False with ==.

For an advanced course, chapter 2 is best taught as decision-making in real Python: truthiness and short-circuit evaluation as working tools, chained comparisons and conditional expressions as idioms, and the match statement as the modern alternative to long elif chains.

Python 3.10 added structural pattern matching: a match statement compares a value against successive case patterns, closer to pattern matching than to the switch statement of C or Java. Python 3.14 adopted PEP 765, which disallows return, break and continue that exit a finally block.

The chapter text named ideas that a learner could not look up in the corpus itself: the None value, containers and their emptiness, identity and the is operator, the order of strings, the arity of an operator, truth tables, operands and the result of and and or, precedence among not, and and or, keywords and soft keywords, indentation and the clause, the assignment expression, the wildcard, sequence and guard patterns, singletons, flowcharts, the exception and the traceback; and this record's own inventory listed block, the Boolean operators and the flow control statement (C_12, C_11, C_13) without the domain ontology carrying their parts. The Python glossary was read for the statement, the suite, the sequence and the singleton; the lexical analysis reference for indentation, tokens and keywords; the data model for identity and None; the built-in constants and functions for None, True, False and ord; the exceptions documentation and the tutorial chapter on errors for the exception, the traceback and the error kinds; the sys documentation for sys.exit; the keyword module for hard and soft keywords; the simple statements reference for pass; What's New in Python 3.10 for the match statement and PEP 572 for the assignment expression. Each concept section of document 1.1.0 is written from those texts, and each of its code claims is executed under CPython 3.14.4 and 3.12.11.

nodes.label: Value
nodes.body: Chapter 1 introduced the value as a piece of data that a program can compute with, and it named three kinds of value: integers, floating-point numbers and strings. Chapter 2 adds a fourth kind, the Boolean value, which has only two members, True and False, and which answers a yes-or-no question (Sweigart, 2025). This branch of the chapter collects what concerns such values: what they are, how Python spells them, and how any other value can be asked whether it counts as true or as false.

paras.text: Chapter 1 introduced the value as a piece of data that a program can compute with, and it named three kinds of value: integers, floating-point numbers and strings. Chapter 2 adds a fourth kind, the Boolean value, which has only two members, True and False, and which answers a yes-or-no question (Sweigart, 2025). This branch of the chapter collects what concerns such values: what they are, how Python spells them, and how any other value can be asked whether it counts as true or as false.

A program that only calculates and prints follows the same path every time it runs. Real programs choose: they show one message to a child and another to an adult, or they accept a password and refuse another. A choice needs a question with exactly two possible answers, and the Boolean value is the answer to such a question. Almost every later chapter depends on it, because loops, searches and error handling all continue or stop according to a true or false value.

Boolean values appear as the result of every comparison, as the operands of the operators and, or and not, and as the condition that follows the word if. They also appear in less obvious places. Python lets any value, not only True and False, stand where a true or false value is expected, so that an empty string or the number zero counts as false while nearly everything else counts as true (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The branch has four sections. The Boolean value is the strict case, with exactly two members. Truthiness widens the idea so that any value can be tested. The value None, which stands for the absence of a value, and the sequences and collections, which can be empty, are the two groups of values whose truth is needed most often. Later branches of the chapter show how comparisons produce these values, how Boolean operators combine them and how flow control statements use them to choose which instructions run.

The two Boolean values must be written exactly as Python spells them, with a capital first letter and without quotation marks. The word true in lowercase is not a Boolean value, and the text 'True' in quotation marks is a string, which Python treats as a different value (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Truth value
nodes.body: Truth values are the values that answer a yes-or-no question. They include the two Boolean values True and False, the special value None that stands for the absence of a value, and the rule by which every other value can also be read as true or false. This second level of the branch gathers the ideas that a learner needs before comparisons and decisions make sense: the Boolean type, the notion of truthiness, the value None and the sequences and collections whose emptiness decides their truth.

paras.text: Truth values are the values that answer a yes-or-no question. They include the two Boolean values True and False, the special value None that stands for the absence of a value, and the rule by which every other value can also be read as true or false. This second level of the branch gathers the ideas that a learner needs before comparisons and decisions make sense: the Boolean type, the notion of truthiness, the value None and the sequences and collections whose emptiness decides their truth.

Truth is the currency of flow control, because every decision that a program makes reduces to a true or false value (Sweigart, 2025). A program can only be read correctly by someone who knows which values count as true. A condition does not have to be a Boolean value, since Python accepts any value in its place and decides for itself whether it is true (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The sections that follow go from the narrow to the wide. The Boolean value is the strict case. Truthiness widens it to every value that Python can test. The value None and the sequences and collections come last, because they are the values whose truth a program most often needs to read, and the last section explains what a sequence or a collection is, since the earlier sections have to use those words.

The widening is written into the language's own types. The two Boolean values are whole numbers as well, so True == 1 and False == 0 both evaluate to True and isinstance(True, int) evaluates to True, because bool is defined as a subclass of int (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Truthiness then covers everything else: bool(0), bool(''), bool([]) and bool(None) all evaluate to False, while bool(0.1) and bool('False') both evaluate to True, which is why a string that reads False is nevertheless a true value.

nodes.label: Boolean value
nodes.body: A Boolean value is a value of the data type bool, and that type has exactly two members, True and False. Where the integer, floating-point and string types have an unlimited number of possible values, the Boolean type has only these two (Sweigart, 2025). The Python documentation states the same fact by saying that the bool type has exactly two constant instances, True and False (Python Software Foundation, 2026); an instance of a type is simply one of its objects, so there are exactly two Boolean objects.

paras.text: A Boolean value is a value of the data type bool, and that type has exactly two members, True and False. Where the integer, floating-point and string types have an unlimited number of possible values, the Boolean type has only these two (Sweigart, 2025). The Python documentation states the same fact by saying that the bool type has exactly two constant instances, True and False (Python Software Foundation, 2026); an instance of a type is simply one of its objects, so there are exactly two Boolean objects.

Two members are exactly what a yes-or-no question needs. Every decision that a program makes, however elaborate its reasons, comes down to one of these two answers, and the flow control statements of this chapter do nothing except choose between instructions according to which answer they receive. The type is named after the mathematician George Boole, which explains why both the name of the type and its two values begin with a capital letter (Sweigart, 2025).

Boolean values are rarely typed in directly; they mostly arrive as results. The comparison 42 == 42 evaluates to True, the comparison 42 == 99 evaluates to False, and the operators and, or and not produce Boolean values from other Boolean values. A Boolean value can also be stored in a variable like any other value, as in spam = True, and the textbook enters exactly that line in the interactive shell (Sweigart, 2025).

In source code the two values are written True and False, each with a capital first letter, without quotation marks and with the rest of the word in lowercase (Sweigart, 2025). They are keywords of the language, an idea that the section on keywords explains, and for that reason an assignment to either of them is illegal and raises a SyntaxError (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Under Python 3.14 the line False = 2 + 2 is rejected with the message cannot assign to False. The type bool is also a subtype of the integer type, so Boolean values behave like 0 and 1 in almost all contexts, the exception being conversion to text (Python Software Foundation, 2026): True + True evaluates to 2 and int(True) evaluates to 1, while str(True) gives the text 'True'.

The capital letter is not a matter of style. The lowercase word true is not a Boolean value but an unknown name, and entering it produces a NameError with the message name 'true' is not defined. Quotation marks change the meaning just as much: the string 'True' is text, and the comparison 'True' == True evaluates to False. Because True counts as 1, an expression such as True + True is legal, but it is rarely what a reader expects and is best avoided.

nodes.definition: The two Boolean values, written with a capital first letter and no quotation marks; every comparison produces one.

nodes.label: Truthiness
nodes.body: Truthiness is the property of every Python value of being counted as true or as false when a Boolean value is needed. The documentation states the principle directly: any object can be tested for truth value, for use in a condition or as an operand of the Boolean operations (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A value that Python counts as true is therefore not necessarily True, and a value that it counts as false is not necessarily False.

paras.text: Truthiness is the property of every Python value of being counted as true or as false when a Boolean value is needed. The documentation states the principle directly: any object can be tested for truth value, for use in a condition or as an operand of the Boolean operations (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A value that Python counts as true is therefore not necessarily True, and a value that it counts as false is not necessarily False.

Without this rule a program would have to compare each value with something before it could decide anything, for example by asking whether a name equals the empty string. With the rule the value itself can serve as the test, so that a program can ask directly whether the user typed anything, whether a result was found or whether a group of items has any members. The style guide of the language relies on exactly this when it recommends the plain test over a comparison with True (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

Truthiness operates wherever Python expects a condition: after the word if, as an operand of and, or and not, and in the built-in function bool, which converts any value to True or False (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It is the reason that a line such as if name: runs its block for a non-empty string and skips it for an empty one.

By default an object is considered true unless it belongs to a short list of exceptions (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The values counted as false are the constants None and False, zero of any numeric type, such as 0 and 0.0, and the empty sequences and collections '', (), [], {} and set(). Everything else is true. The function bool shows the rule at work: bool('') evaluates to False, bool(0.0) evaluates to False, and bool(' ') evaluates to True because a string that holds one space is not empty.

Truth is decided by emptiness or zero, never by what the content says. The string '0' and the string 'False' are both non-empty and therefore true: bool('0') evaluates to True and bool('False') evaluates to True. A list that contains a zero is not empty either, so bool([0]) evaluates to True. Truthiness is also not equality: the empty list counts as false when it is tested, yet the comparison [] == False evaluates to False because a list and a Boolean value are different values. Programmers who define their own kinds of object can decide how those objects are read, which is a subject for later chapters.

nodes.definition: Any value can be tested for truth: None, False, zero and empty sequences are false, so bool('') is False while bool('0') is True.

nodes.label: None value
nodes.body: None is a built-in value that represents the absence of a value. The documentation describes it as an object frequently used to represent the absence of a value, and as the sole instance of the type NoneType, which means that it is the only object of that type (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It is written None, with a capital N and without quotation marks, in the same way as True and False.

paras.text: None is a built-in value that represents the absence of a value. The documentation describes it as an object frequently used to represent the absence of a value, and as the sole instance of the type NoneType, which means that it is the only object of that type (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It is written None, with a capital N and without quotation marks, in the same way as True and False.

A program often has to say that nothing is there yet without inventing a number or a string for the purpose. Zero and the empty string already mean something, so they make poor markers of absence, and None is a distinct value that cannot be mistaken for them. A variable that has not yet received a real answer can hold None, and a function that finds nothing can hand it back.

None is what a function produces when it does not return anything explicitly; the language reference says it is returned from functions that don't explicitly return anything (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The function print is such a function, so the expression print() is None evaluates to True, after printing an empty line. None is also the value that conditions on missing data are written against, as in the test x is None.

There is exactly one None in a running program. The call type(None) reports <class 'NoneType'>, and the language reference states that its truth value is false (Python Software Foundation, 2026), so bool(None) evaluates to False and the expression None or 'default' evaluates to 'default'. Because the value is unique, the program can recognise it by identity, with the operator is, which the section on identity comparison explains.

None is false, but it is not equal to False and not equal to zero: None == False evaluates to False and None == 0 evaluates to False. The style guide asks that comparisons with None be made with is or is not and never with the equality operators (Van Rossum et al., 2001). It also warns against writing if x when the intention was if x is not None, because the other value might be a container that happens to be empty, and an empty container counts as false (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

nodes.definition: The single built-in value that stands for the absence of a value; it counts as false but is not equal to False.

nodes.label: Sequence and collection
nodes.body: A sequence is an ordered group of items that can be reached by position and that has a length. The string of Chapter 1 is a sequence of characters, and the glossary names list, str, tuple and bytes (a sequence of byte values) as the built-in sequence types (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A list is written with square brackets, as in [10, 20, 30], and a tuple is written with parentheses, as in (10, 20, 30). A collection is the wider word for any object that holds other values, so it also covers the dictionary, which maps keys to values, and the set, which holds each distinct item once and has no order (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A sequence is an ordered group of items that can be reached by position and that has a length. The string of Chapter 1 is a sequence of characters, and the glossary names list, str, tuple and bytes (a sequence of byte values) as the built-in sequence types (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A list is written with square brackets, as in [10, 20, 30], and a tuple is written with parentheses, as in (10, 20, 30). A collection is the wider word for any object that holds other values, so it also covers the dictionary, which maps keys to values, and the set, which holds each distinct item once and has no order (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The chapter needs these words because the rule for truth refers to them: empty sequences and collections count as false. A program often needs to know whether a group has any members at all, for example whether a search found anything or whether the user entered a value, and the emptiness of a group is the simplest way to say so.

Sequences and collections are everywhere in real programs, and later chapters of the course treat lists and dictionaries in detail. In this chapter they matter in two places: when the truth of a value is tested, and when the match statement compares a value against patterns that describe a sequence.

The function len from Chapter 1 reports the number of items, so len([10, 20, 30]) evaluates to 3 and len('') evaluates to 0. An empty group is written '' for a string, [] for a list, () for a tuple, set() for a set and {} for a dictionary: empty braces create a dictionary, and type({}) reports <class 'dict'>, which is why the empty set needs a function call of its own. Each of these empty values counts as false.

A group counts as false only when it is empty. A group of one item is true even if that item is itself false or empty: bool([0]) evaluates to True and bool([[]]) evaluates to True, because the outer list holds one item. The truth of a group says nothing about the truth of its members.

nodes.definition: A sequence or collection such as a string, list, tuple, dictionary or set; when it is empty it counts as false.

nodes.label: Comparison
nodes.body: A comparison is an expression that asks a question about two values and answers with a Boolean value. The textbook calls the operators that write such questions comparison operators or, by a second name, relational operators, and it lists six of them: ==, !=, <, >, <= and >= (Sweigart, 2025). The reference documentation counts eight comparison operations, because it adds the two identity operators is and is not to the six (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A comparison is an expression that asks a question about two values and answers with a Boolean value. The textbook calls the operators that write such questions comparison operators or, by a second name, relational operators, and it lists six of them: ==, !=, <, >, <= and >= (Sweigart, 2025). The reference documentation counts eight comparison operations, because it adds the two identity operators is and is not to the six (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A program cannot decide anything without information about its data, and comparisons are how data is turned into the true-or-false answer that a decision needs. They ask whether a name equals the expected one, whether an age lies below a limit, or whether two variables hold the same value. Comparing two literal values, that is, two values written directly in the program such as 'dog' and 'cat', is rarely useful, because the answer is always the same; comparisons earn their place when at least one side is a variable (Sweigart, 2025).

Comparisons are written in the condition of every if and elif statement, and they are the usual operands of the Boolean operators and, or and not. The examples of the chapter compare a name with 'Alice', an age with 12, and a stored number with 42. A comparison is an expression like any other, so its value can also be printed or stored in a variable.

Every comparison operator takes two operands and evaluates to True or False (Sweigart, 2025). All comparison operators have the same priority, and that priority is lower than the priority of any arithmetic operator (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In 2 + 2 == 4 the addition is therefore evaluated first, and the comparison then asks whether 4 equals 4. The branch is divided into equality comparisons, which ask whether two values are the same, and ordering comparisons, which ask which of two values comes first.

A comparison produces a Boolean value, not a decision: nothing happens until a flow control statement acts on the result. Unless stated otherwise, objects of different types never compare equal (Python Software Foundation, 2026), but the numeric types are an exception, so 42 == 42.0 evaluates to True while 42 == '42' evaluates to False.

nodes.label: Equality comparison
nodes.body: Equality comparisons ask whether two values are the same. The two operators for the purpose are == and !=, which compare the values of their operands, and the identity operators is and is not, which ask the different question of whether two expressions refer to one and the same object (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The branch also treats the frequent confusion between the equality operator == and the assignment operator =.

paras.text: Equality comparisons ask whether two values are the same. The two operators for the purpose are == and !=, which compare the values of their operands, and the identity operators is and is not, which ask the different question of whether two expressions refer to one and the same object (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The branch also treats the frequent confusion between the equality operator == and the assignment operator =.

Equality is the question that programs ask most often: whether the user typed the expected word, whether a number reached an exact target, whether a value is the special value None. The three questions look similar and need three different tools, and choosing the wrong one produces programs that run but answer incorrectly.

The sections of the branch take the value comparison first, then the difference between == and =, and finally the identity comparison. The first two use the textbook's own examples; the third comes from the style guide, which asks that some comparisons be made with is (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

The three questions come apart on real values, and each failure looks different. The comparison [1, 2] == [1, 2] evaluates to True while [1, 2] is [1, 2] evaluates to False, because the two lists hold the same items in two different objects (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Writing one equals sign where two were meant is caught earlier still: the line if spam = 42: never runs at all, since Python refuses the file with a SyntaxError whose message asks whether == or := was meant. Only the first two mistakes can be found by reading what a program printed.

nodes.label: Equality
nodes.body: The equality operators compare two values. The operator == (equal to) evaluates to True when the values on both sides are the same, and the operator != (not equal to) evaluates to True when the two values are different (Sweigart, 2025). Both operators return a Boolean value and neither changes the values it compares.

paras.text: The equality operators compare two values. The operator == (equal to) evaluates to True when the values on both sides are the same, and the operator != (not equal to) evaluates to True when the two values are different (Sweigart, 2025). Both operators return a Boolean value and neither changes the values it compares.

Equality is how a program recognises what it was given: the right name, the right answer, the expected command. Since the result is always True or False, an equality comparison is the usual form of the condition that follows if and elif.

The textbook enters the operators in the interactive shell: 42 == 42 evaluates to True, 42 == 99 evaluates to False, 2 != 3 evaluates to True and 2 != 2 evaluates to False. In programs the typical line compares a variable with a value, as in name == 'Alice' (Sweigart, 2025).

The operators work with values of any data type (Sweigart, 2025). Strings are compared character by character and capitals count, so 'hello' == 'hello' evaluates to True while 'hello' == 'Hello' evaluates to False. Numbers are compared by their value even when their types differ, so 42 == 42.0 evaluates to True, because Python considers the integer 42 to be the same as the float 42.0 (Sweigart, 2025); the documentation adds that numbers of the built-in numeric types compare mathematically correctly within and across their types (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Values of other, unrelated types are never equal, and no error is raised: the integer 42 does not equal the string '42', so 42 == '42' evaluates to False.

Equality of floating-point numbers needs care. Because floats are stored in binary, the comparison 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 evaluates to False, and a program that tests a calculated float for exact equality may never find the answer it expects. The operator != is the exact opposite of ==, so a mistaken == cannot be repaired by reading the result backwards.

nodes.definition: == and != compare values; an integer never equals a string, so 42 == '42' is False.

nodes.label: Equality versus assignment
nodes.body: The symbols == and = look alike and do entirely different things. The textbook states the difference in two sentences: the == operator asks whether two values are the same as each other, and the = operator puts the value on the right into the variable on the left (Sweigart, 2025). The first is a comparison and produces a Boolean value; the second is an assignment, which Chapter 1 introduced as a statement that stores a value.

paras.text: The symbols == and = look alike and do entirely different things. The textbook states the difference in two sentences: the == operator asks whether two values are the same as each other, and the = operator puts the value on the right into the variable on the left (Sweigart, 2025). The first is a comparison and produces a Boolean value; the second is an assignment, which Chapter 1 introduced as a statement that stores a value.

The two are easy to confuse, and the confusion is expensive: a condition that was meant to ask a question would instead try to store something, and a statement that was meant to store something would only ask a question and discard the answer. A learner who keeps the distinction clear avoids a whole family of errors before they happen.

The confusion appears in the condition of an if statement, where a beginner writes one equals sign instead of two, and in the line that was meant to be an assignment but was typed as a comparison. The textbook offers a way to remember which is which: the == operator consists of two characters, just like the != operator, and both are comparisons (Sweigart, 2025).

A comparison is an expression, so 4 == 2 + 2 evaluates to True, with the addition done first. An assignment is a statement, so it produces no value to print. Python guards against the most common slip. Writing if x = 3: after x has been assigned raises a SyntaxError with the message invalid syntax. Maybe you meant '==' or ':=' instead of '='?, and the second operator in that message is the assignment expression explained in the branch on expression forms.

The guard works only where an assignment cannot be valid. The reverse slip, writing == where = was meant, is a legal line that silently does nothing useful, for example spam == 4 on a line by itself, so only careful reading finds it.

nodes.definition: The operator == asks whether two values are the same; the operator = puts the value on its right into the variable on its left.

nodes.label: Identity comparison
nodes.body: An identity comparison asks whether two expressions refer to one and the same object, not merely to equal values. The operator is evaluates to True for the same object and is not evaluates to True for different objects; the documentation lists them as object identity and negated object identity (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Every object has an identity, and the built-in function id reports it as an integer that is unique and constant for the object during its lifetime (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: An identity comparison asks whether two expressions refer to one and the same object, not merely to equal values. The operator is evaluates to True for the same object and is not evaluates to True for different objects; the documentation lists them as object identity and negated object identity (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Every object has an identity, and the built-in function id reports it as an integer that is unique and constant for the object during its lifetime (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Identity matters for values that exist only once. The reference documentation calls None a singleton, an object of which exactly one exists, and records that the style guide advises comparing singletons with is or is not, never with the equality operators (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The behaviour of is cannot be customised, and it never raises an exception when it is applied to two objects, which makes it the dependable way to ask whether a value is the value None (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The everyday use is the test x is None, which asks whether a variable holds the absence of a value. The style guide also asks for the form x is not None instead of not x is None, because the two are equivalent but the first reads better (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

Two separate objects can be equal without being identical. After a = [1, 2], b = [1, 2] and c = a, the lists a and b have equal values and are different objects, while c is simply a second name for the object a. The program that prints a == b, a is b and a is c therefore prints True False True.

The operator is is not a stricter ==, and it must not be used to compare numbers or text. Use == to ask whether values are equal and keep is for None, as the style guide advises (Van Rossum et al., 2001). The two operators answer different questions, and a program that mixes them up can work in a test and fail with other data.

nodes.definition: The operators is and is not ask whether two expressions are the very same object, which is a different question from whether their values are equal.

nodes.label: Ordering comparison
nodes.body: Ordering comparisons ask which of two values comes first. The four operators are < (less than), > (greater than), <= (less than or equal to) and >= (greater than or equal to) (Sweigart, 2025). Python also lets several of them be chained in one expression, so that a range can be written the way it is written in mathematics, and it applies the same operators to strings.

paras.text: Ordering comparisons ask which of two values comes first. The four operators are < (less than), > (greater than), <= (less than or equal to) and >= (greater than or equal to) (Sweigart, 2025). Python also lets several of them be chained in one expression, so that a range can be written the way it is written in mathematics, and it applies the same operators to strings.

Programs are full of thresholds and limits: an age under twelve, a stock level at least ten, a price not above a budget. Ordering comparisons express each of them in one operator. Because they all return a Boolean value, they join with equality comparisons and with the Boolean operators into conditions of any size.

The section on ordering shows the four operators on numbers, the section on chained comparison shows how two ordering questions can be asked at once, and the section on string ordering shows that the same operators work on text, by a rule that surprises beginners. The textbook shows the operators on integer and floating-point values (Sweigart, 2025); the reference documentation adds the other cases (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The rule that surprises beginners is the one for text. Strings are compared character by character by the Unicode code point of each character, so 'apple' < 'banana' evaluates to True as expected, but 'Zoe' < 'alice' evaluates to True as well, because every capital letter has a smaller code point than every small letter (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A chain is not two comparisons written side by side either: in 12 < len(name) < 20 the middle expression is evaluated once, and the chain stops at the first link that is false.

nodes.label: Ordering
nodes.body: The ordering operators compare two values by size. The operator < is true when the first value is smaller, > when it is larger, <= when it is smaller or equal, and >= when it is larger or equal (Sweigart, 2025). Each returns True or False, so 42 < 100 evaluates to True and 42 > 100 evaluates to False.

paras.text: The ordering operators compare two values by size. The operator < is true when the first value is smaller, > when it is larger, <= when it is smaller or equal, and >= when it is larger or equal (Sweigart, 2025). Each returns True or False, so 42 < 100 evaluates to True and 42 > 100 evaluates to False.

Thresholds are everywhere in programs, and every threshold is an ordering comparison: whether someone is old enough for a ticket class, whether a count has reached a limit, whether a result is above zero. The distinction between strict and non-strict forms decides whether the boundary value itself belongs to the range.

The textbook compares a variable with a value, as in eggs <= 42 and my_age >= 10, and it uses the operator in the conditions of its ticket-style examples, such as age < 12 and age > 100 (Sweigart, 2025). Integers and floats can be mixed freely, so 1.999 < 5 evaluates to True.

The operators ask a question about order, and the answer depends only on the two values: 42 < 42 evaluates to False because a value is not smaller than itself, while 42 <= 42 evaluates to True. The textbook shows these operators on integer and floating-point values (Sweigart, 2025), and the reference documentation records that they are only defined where they make sense (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Where they do not, Python refuses instead of guessing: 3 < '4' raises a TypeError with the message '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'str'.

The most common mistake is choosing the wrong boundary. The textbook admits that all true programmers have at some point spent an hour finding out that their program does not work because they typed < instead of <= (Sweigart, 2025). When a condition seems to fail only for one exact value, check whether the operator should include its boundary.

nodes.definition: <, >, <= and >= compare order and return a Boolean value.

error.out: TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'str'

nodes.label: Chained comparison
nodes.body: A chained comparison joins several comparison operators in one expression, so that x < y <= z asks both questions at once. The reference documentation defines it as equivalent to x < y and y <= z, except that y is evaluated only once (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In general a op1 b op2 c is equivalent to a op1 b and b op2 c, with each expression evaluated at most once (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A chained comparison joins several comparison operators in one expression, so that x < y <= z asks both questions at once. The reference documentation defines it as equivalent to x < y and y <= z, except that y is evaluated only once (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In general a op1 b op2 c is equivalent to a op1 b and b op2 c, with each expression evaluated at most once (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Chaining lets a program write a range check the way mathematics writes it. The condition that an age lies from 12 up to but not including 65 becomes 12 <= age < 65 and not the longer 12 <= age and age < 65. The short form is easier to read and cannot be broken by changing the variable name in only one half.

Chained comparisons are used in conditions that test whether a value lies in an interval, such as the age bands of a ticket price or a score between two limits. They are a feature of Python that many other languages lack, and the textbook does not introduce them, so a learner meets them first in the documentation and in other people's code.

Python evaluates the chain from left to right and stops as soon as one comparison is false. The expression 1 < 2 < 3 evaluates to True and 3 > 2 > 5 evaluates to False. The stopping rule is visible when a later operand would fail: 5 < 3 < 1/0 evaluates to False without raising a ZeroDivisionError, because the first comparison is already false and the third operand is never evaluated (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A chain does not compare its outer values with each other: a op1 b op2 c implies no comparison between a and c, so x < y > z is legal, though perhaps not pretty (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and 1 < 2 > 1.5 evaluates to True. Reading a mixed chain as a statement about its two ends is a mistake.

nodes.definition: Comparisons chain: x < y <= z means x < y and y <= z, with y evaluated once.

nodes.label: String ordering
nodes.body: String ordering is the use of <, >, <= and >= on text. The reference documentation says that strings compare lexicographically, that is, character by character from the left as in a dictionary, using the numerical Unicode code points of their characters (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Unicode is the standard that gives every character a number, called its code point. The code point of a character is its ordinal value, the number that the built-in function ord reports (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook describes the ordering operators for integer and floating-point values only (Sweigart, 2025), so this is a case where the documentation says more than the book.

paras.text: String ordering is the use of <, >, <= and >= on text. The reference documentation says that strings compare lexicographically, that is, character by character from the left as in a dictionary, using the numerical Unicode code points of their characters (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Unicode is the standard that gives every character a number, called its code point. The code point of a character is its ordinal value, the number that the built-in function ord reports (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook describes the ordering operators for integer and floating-point values only (Sweigart, 2025), so this is a case where the documentation says more than the book.

Sorting names, checking whether a word comes before another and arranging records all depend on comparing text. A learner who expects the order of a dictionary will be surprised by the order that Python uses, and the surprise is the source of many bugs, which is the programmers' word for faults in a program, in code that sorts text.

String ordering appears whenever text is placed in order, for example when names are compared, and it explains the order in which sorted text appears. It is also the reason why digits stored as text cannot be compared as numbers.

Python compares the first characters, and only if they are equal does it look at the second ones. The comparison 'apple' < 'banana' evaluates to True because ord('a') is 97 and ord('b') is 98. The capital letters have smaller code points than the lowercase ones, since ord('Z') is 90, so 'Z' < 'a' evaluates to True and 'apple' < 'Apple' evaluates to False.

The order is that of the code points, not of a human alphabet. The text '10' < '9' evaluates to True because the character '1' comes before '9', although the number 10 is larger than 9, so numbers that arrive as text must be converted before they are compared. The documentation also warns that a character with an accent can be written in more than one way, so that two strings that look identical may compare as different (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.definition: Strings compare lexicographically by the code points of their characters, so every capital letter comes before every lowercase one.

nodes.label: Boolean operation
nodes.body: Boolean operations combine truth values into new truth values. Python has three Boolean operators, and, or and not. The textbook introduces them as the operators used to compare Boolean values, which, like the comparison operators, evaluate an expression down to a Boolean value (Sweigart, 2025). The reference documentation calls them the Boolean operations and adds a detail that the textbook leaves out: and and or return one of their operands, which is not always a plain True or False (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: Boolean operations combine truth values into new truth values. Python has three Boolean operators, and, or and not. The textbook introduces them as the operators used to compare Boolean values, which, like the comparison operators, evaluate an expression down to a Boolean value (Sweigart, 2025). The reference documentation calls them the Boolean operations and adds a detail that the textbook leaves out: and and or return one of their operands, which is not always a plain True or False (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A single comparison answers a single question, but real decisions are rarely so simple. A ticket is free when the visitor is under twelve or over sixty-five, and a login succeeds when the name matches and the password matches. Boolean operators build such compound conditions out of simple ones, and without them every combination of facts would need a decision of its own nested inside another.

Boolean operators appear in the condition of an if or elif statement, usually joining comparisons. The second short program of the chapter uses or so that the unit of a hard drive is recognised whether the user types it in uppercase or in lowercase (Sweigart, 2025). Anywhere that a program wants to say 'this and that', 'this or that' or 'not this', it uses one of the three.

The branch has two parts. The logical operators are explained one at a time, together with the number of operands each takes and the truth table that lists every possible result. The evaluation section then explains how Python works through a compound expression: from left to right, stopping as soon as the answer is known, returning one of the operands, mixing in comparisons, and giving not priority over and and and priority over or.

The rule that Boolean operators always produce True or False is correct only when their operands are themselves True or False. With other values, and and or hand back one of the operands, and the documentation names this as an important exception to the rule that operations with a Boolean result return True or False (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Logical operator
nodes.body: The logical operators are and, or and not. The first two join two truth values, and the third reverses one. Together they cover the three basic ways of reasoning about yes and no: requiring that both facts hold, requiring that at least one holds, and asking that a fact does not hold (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The logical operators are and, or and not. The first two join two truth values, and the third reverses one. Together they cover the three basic ways of reasoning about yes and no: requiring that both facts hold, requiring that at least one holds, and asking that a fact does not hold (Sweigart, 2025).

Every compound condition in a program is built from these three words, so a precise knowledge of what each does is the foundation for reading and writing conditions. Their meanings are fixed by tables of results, which makes them easy to check completely.

The branch explains each operator in turn, with the examples of the textbook, and then two ideas that describe them all: the number of operands an operator takes, which separates not from and and or, and the truth table, a complete list of the results an operator can give.

The tables are small enough to hold in full, which is the point of them. Each of and and or has four rows, one for every pairing of two truth values, and not has two, so ten rows describe the three operators completely (Sweigart, 2025). The count is also why their order matters: not binds more tightly than the other two, so not True and False evaluates to False, which is the reading (not True) and False, while not (True and False) evaluates to True instead.

nodes.label: And operator
nodes.body: The and operator joins two Boolean values or expressions and evaluates to True only if both of them are True; otherwise it evaluates to False (Sweigart, 2025). Because it always takes two operands, the textbook calls it a binary Boolean operator.

paras.text: The and operator joins two Boolean values or expressions and evaluates to True only if both of them are True; otherwise it evaluates to False (Sweigart, 2025). Because it always takes two operands, the textbook calls it a binary Boolean operator.

The operator expresses a requirement that all of several conditions hold at once: the name is correct and the password is correct, the visitor is an adult and has a ticket. A single failing part is enough to make the whole condition false, which is exactly the behaviour that a security check or an eligibility rule needs.

The textbook enters True and True, which evaluates to True, and True and False, which evaluates to False. It also joins comparisons, so (4 < 5) and (5 < 6) evaluates to True while (4 < 5) and (9 < 6) evaluates to False, because the second comparison fails (Sweigart, 2025).

Python evaluates the left operand first. According to the reference documentation, x and y first evaluates x; if x is false, its value is returned, and otherwise y is evaluated and its value is returned (Python Software Foundation, 2026). For Boolean operands that rule gives the same answers as the table of results: the four combinations True and True, True and False, False and True and False and False evaluate to True, False, False and False in that order.

Each side of and must be a complete expression. A programmer who has a range in mind may write age > 12 and < 65, which Python rejects as a SyntaxError with the message invalid syntax; the correct line repeats the variable, as in age > 12 and age < 65, or uses a chained comparison. Remember also that and can return an operand instead of a Boolean value, as the section on operand results shows.

nodes.definition: and is true only when both operands are true.

nodes.label: Or operator
nodes.body: The or operator joins two Boolean values or expressions and evaluates to True if either of them is True. Only when both are False does it evaluate to False (Sweigart, 2025). Like and, it takes two operands and is therefore a binary Boolean operator.

paras.text: The or operator joins two Boolean values or expressions and evaluates to True if either of them is True. Only when both are False does it evaluate to False (Sweigart, 2025). Like and, it takes two operands and is therefore a binary Boolean operator.

The operator expresses alternatives: any one of several conditions is enough. It lets a program accept several spellings of the same answer, or apply one rule to several groups, without repeating the action for each of them.

The textbook enters False or True, which evaluates to True, and False or False, which evaluates to False, and it combines comparisons, so (1 == 2) or (2 == 2) evaluates to True. The second short program of the chapter uses the test unit == 'TB' or unit == 'tb' so that the program works whether the user enters the unit in uppercase or in lowercase (Sweigart, 2025).

Python evaluates the left operand first. The reference documentation states that x or y first evaluates x; if x is true, its value is returned, and otherwise y is evaluated and its value is returned (Python Software Foundation, 2026). For Boolean operands this is the same as the table of results: only the combination False or False evaluates to False.

A classic mistake is to write the second comparison in a shortened form, such as unit == 'TB' or 'tb'. The right-hand operand 'tb' is a non-empty string, which counts as true, so the whole condition is true whatever the unit is: with the unit 'GB' the expression evaluates to 'tb', which an if statement reads as true. Each alternative needs its own complete comparison.

nodes.definition: or is true when either operand is true.

nodes.label: Not operator
nodes.body: The not operator reverses a truth value. Unlike and and or, it operates on only one Boolean value or expression, which makes it a unary operator, and it evaluates to the opposite Boolean value (Sweigart, 2025). The expression not True evaluates to False, and not False evaluates to True.

paras.text: The not operator reverses a truth value. Unlike and and or, it operates on only one Boolean value or expression, which makes it a unary operator, and it evaluates to the opposite Boolean value (Sweigart, 2025). The expression not True evaluates to False, and not False evaluates to True.

Many conditions are most naturally stated as a negation: the file is not found, the list is not empty, the answer is not yes. The operator also reverses a stored flag in a single step, which is how the Opposite Day program of the textbook flips its variable.

The textbook shows that not can be repeated, in the way a double negative can in speech, so not not not not True evaluates to True, and adds that there is never a real reason to do this in programs (Sweigart, 2025). In real code the operator usually appears in front of a comparison or a variable that holds a Boolean value.

The reference documentation defines it by cases: the operator not yields True if its argument is false and False otherwise (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Because not has to create a new value, it always returns a Boolean value, whatever the type of its argument: not 'foo' produces False and not '' produces True. It also has a lower priority than the comparison operators, so not 4 == 5 is read as not (4 == 5) and evaluates to True (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The operator belongs in front of an expression, never inside a comparison. Writing 4 == not 5 is a SyntaxError with the message invalid syntax, and the documentation states that a == not b is a syntax error (Python Software Foundation, 2026). When a negation is hard to read, a parenthesis or a reversed comparison, such as != instead of not ... ==, is clearer.

nodes.definition: not inverts a single Boolean value.

nodes.label: Binary and unary operators
nodes.body: The arity of an operator is the number of operands that it takes. A binary operator takes two, one on each side, and a unary operator takes one. In the Boolean operators, and and or are binary, whereas not is unary (Sweigart, 2025). The reference documentation states the general convention that, unless the syntax is explicitly given, the operators in its precedence table are binary (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: The arity of an operator is the number of operands that it takes. A binary operator takes two, one on each side, and a unary operator takes one. In the Boolean operators, and and or are binary, whereas not is unary (Sweigart, 2025). The reference documentation states the general convention that, unless the syntax is explicitly given, the operators in its precedence table are binary (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Knowing how many operands an operator wants explains many error messages and many reading mistakes. An operator with a missing operand cannot be evaluated, and an operator that applies to one operand binds to whatever follows it, which decides what a negation reverses.

A symbol can serve in both roles. The minus sign is binary in 5 - 3, which subtracts, and unary in -(2 + 3), which the documentation describes as yielding the negation of its numeric argument, so the expression evaluates to -5 (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Chapter 1 met the same sign in -3 ** 2, where it is unary.

A binary operator can be repeated to join many operands, because each use takes the result of the one before it: a and b and c is read as (a and b) and c. A unary operator applies to the single expression on its right. This is why not 2 + 2 == 5 reverses the whole comparison and not only the number 2: the unary not takes everything that binds more tightly than itself.

Do not read a unary operator as a binary one. The expression 4 - -2 contains a binary minus sign followed by a unary one and evaluates to 6, which many readers do not expect at first sight. When a line mixes the two uses, parentheses show the reader which is which, as in 4 - (-2).

nodes.definition: A binary operator takes two operands and a unary operator takes one; and and or are binary, not is unary.

nodes.label: Truth table
nodes.body: A truth table shows every possible result of a Boolean operator (Sweigart, 2025). Each row lists one combination of values for the operands and the value to which the operator evaluates for that combination. Because a Boolean value has only two possibilities, the number of rows is small and the table is complete.

paras.text: A truth table shows every possible result of a Boolean operator (Sweigart, 2025). Each row lists one combination of values for the operands and the value to which the operator evaluates for that combination. Because a Boolean value has only two possibilities, the number of rows is small and the table is complete.

The table is a full definition of an operator, not an example of it. Nothing about and, or or not remains to be guessed once the table is known, and a learner can check any reading of a compound condition by writing out the rows. The practice questions at the end of the chapter ask the reader to write the tables from memory for exactly this reason (Sweigart, 2025).

The textbook gives three tables, Table 2-2 for and, Table 2-3 for or and Table 2-4 for not (Sweigart, 2025). They are met again in the practice questions at the end of the chapter, and a learner can rebuild them at any time by evaluating the expressions in the interactive shell.

An operator with two Boolean operands has four rows, because each operand can take two values. For and the four rows evaluate to True, False, False and False, for the operands in the order True and True, True and False, False and True, False and False. For or the same rows evaluate to True, True, True and False. The operator not takes one operand, so its table has two rows: not True evaluates to False and not False evaluates to True.

A truth table describes the behaviour of the operators on True and False only. With other kinds of value, and and or return an operand, as the section on operand results explains, and a table written for Boolean values then no longer lists the results. The tables also say nothing about the order in which operands are evaluated, which matters when an operand has an effect of its own.

nodes.definition: A table that lists every possible combination of operand values for a Boolean operator and the result for each.

nodes.label: Evaluation
nodes.body: Evaluation is the process by which Python works out the value of an expression (Python Software Foundation, 2026). For compound Boolean expressions it follows four rules that this branch explains: the operands are evaluated from left to right and evaluation stops as soon as the answer is known, the result can be one of the operands, comparisons and Boolean operators can be mixed freely, and the three Boolean operators have a fixed order of priority.

paras.text: Evaluation is the process by which Python works out the value of an expression (Python Software Foundation, 2026). For compound Boolean expressions it follows four rules that this branch explains: the operands are evaluated from left to right and evaluation stops as soon as the answer is known, the result can be one of the operands, comparisons and Boolean operators can be mixed freely, and the three Boolean operators have a fixed order of priority.

Two readers who follow the same rules reach the same answer, and a program that follows them behaves the way its author intended. The rules also give the operators practical powers beyond the truth tables: a condition can protect a risky calculation, and a default value can replace an empty one.

The sections of this branch go from the mechanism to the rules that govern its use. Short-circuit evaluation and operand results describe what the operators do with their operands, the section on Boolean expressions shows comparisons and Boolean operators together, and the final section gives the order in which not, and and or are applied.

The rules show themselves in what an expression returns rather than in what it decides. The expression 0 or 'default' evaluates to 'default' and '' or 0 evaluates to 0, because or hands back the operand it stopped at and not a Boolean (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Stopping early is what lets a condition protect a risky calculation: with n bound to 0 the expression n != 0 and 100 / n evaluates to False and the division never runs, whereas the same two operands in the other order raise ZeroDivisionError.

nodes.label: Short circuit
nodes.body: Short-circuit evaluation means that the operators and and or evaluate their second operand only when the first operand has not already decided the result. The documentation states it in two notes: or only evaluates the second argument if the first one is false, and and only evaluates the second argument if the first one is true (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: Short-circuit evaluation means that the operators and and or evaluate their second operand only when the first operand has not already decided the result. The documentation states it in two notes: or only evaluates the second argument if the first one is false, and and only evaluates the second argument if the first one is true (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The rule is a safeguard and a saving. A condition can be arranged so that the first operand checks that the second operand is safe to evaluate, and an expensive or risky second operand is skipped whenever the first one settles the answer. Programmers use this to write checks in a single line that would otherwise need a nested decision.

The pattern is found in conditions that guard a division or a lookup, as in x != 0 and 10 / x > 2, and in conditions that supply a fallback. The textbook does not introduce short-circuit evaluation, but its operators behave this way in every program it shows (Sweigart, 2025).

Python evaluates the first operand and looks at its truth. For and, a false first operand settles the result, so the second is not evaluated; for or, a true first operand settles it. The expression 1 or 1 / 0 evaluates to 1 and the expression 0 and 1 / 0 evaluates to 0, and in neither case is the division carried out. When the second operand is needed it is evaluated, so 1 and 1 / 0 raises a ZeroDivisionError. With x = 0, the condition x != 0 and 10 / x > 2 evaluates to False without any error.

Anything that the skipped operand would have done is skipped too. If the second operand is a call to a function that prints, the printing does not happen when the first operand settles the result: False and print('skipped') prints nothing, while True and print('shown') prints shown. A programmer must not rely on a skipped operand to run, and should not hide needed actions inside a condition.

nodes.definition: and and or stop evaluating as soon as the answer is known, so the second operand is sometimes never evaluated.

nodes.label: Operand result
nodes.body: The result of and and or is one of their operands. The reference documentation says that neither operator restricts the value and type it returns to False and True, but rather returns the last evaluated argument (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The rule is that x and y returns x if x is false and y otherwise, and that x or y returns x if x is true and y otherwise.

paras.text: The result of and and or is one of their operands. The reference documentation says that neither operator restricts the value and type it returns to False and True, but rather returns the last evaluated argument (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The rule is that x and y returns x if x is false and y otherwise, and that x or y returns x if x is true and y otherwise.

This behaviour is deliberate and useful. The documentation gives the example of a string that should be replaced by a default value if it is empty: the expression s or 'foo' yields the desired value (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A single operator therefore does the work of a small decision, which is why the idiom is so common in Python code.

The idiom appears wherever an empty or missing value should be replaced by a fallback, for example a name that the user left blank, and in chains of alternatives where the first usable value wins. The operator not is the exception, because it has to create a new value and therefore always returns True or False (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The returned operand is the one that settled the result. The expression 'hi' and 'there' evaluates to 'there', because the first operand is true and the second is the last one evaluated, and '' and 'there' evaluates to '', the first operand, which is already false. In the same way 0 or 'default' evaluates to 'default' and 'set' or 'default' evaluates to 'set'. A chain returns the operand that decides it: 1 and 2 and 3 evaluates to 3 and 0 or [] or None evaluates to None.

When the value is printed or stored, it is the operand and not a Boolean value that is seen. If a strict True or False is needed, the function bool converts the result, as in bool('hi' and 'there'). The surprise is greatest when a condition is shown to a user, because a text such as 'there' appears where the reader expected True.

nodes.definition: and and or return one of their operands, which is not necessarily True or False; not always returns a Boolean value.

nodes.label: Boolean expression
nodes.body: A Boolean expression is an expression whose value is True or False, built from comparisons and Boolean operators. The textbook explains that an expression such as 4 < 5 is not itself a Boolean value, but it is an expression that evaluates down to one, so comparison operators can be used inside expressions with the Boolean operators (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A Boolean expression is an expression whose value is True or False, built from comparisons and Boolean operators. The textbook explains that an expression such as 4 < 5 is not itself a Boolean value, but it is an expression that evaluates down to one, so comparison operators can be used inside expressions with the Boolean operators (Sweigart, 2025).

Real conditions mix both kinds of operator: a value is compared with a limit, and several such comparisons are then joined by and, or and not. Without the ability to mix them, each comparison would have to be stored in a variable before it could be combined.

The textbook enters (4 < 5) and (5 < 6), which evaluates to True, (4 < 5) and (9 < 6), which evaluates to False, and (1 == 2) or (2 == 2), which evaluates to True. The conditions of the programs in the chapter, such as unit == 'TB' or unit == 'tb', have the same form (Sweigart, 2025).

The computer evaluates the left expression first and then the right expression. When it knows the Boolean value of each, it evaluates the whole expression down to one Boolean value (Sweigart, 2025). A longer line follows the same path. With spam = 4, the expression 2 + 2 == spam and not 2 + 2 == (spam + 1) and 2 * 2 == 2 + 2 evaluates to True: the arithmetic comes first, then the comparisons, then not, then and.

Parentheses around the comparisons are not required, but they make a line easier to read, and a long Boolean expression is easier to check when it is split into named parts. A common slip is to forget that the operators work on whole expressions: spam == 3 or 4 does not ask whether spam is 3 or 4, since the 4 on the right is a value that counts as true.

nodes.definition: A comparison evaluates to a Boolean value, so comparisons and Boolean operators can be mixed in one expression.

nodes.label: Boolean precedence
nodes.body: Boolean precedence is the order in which a Python expression applies not, and and or when it contains several of them. The Boolean operators have an order of operations just like the math operators do: after any math and comparison operators evaluate, Python evaluates the not operators first, then the and operators, and then the or operators (Sweigart, 2025). The reference documentation lists the same order from the lowest priority to the highest as or, and, not (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: Boolean precedence is the order in which a Python expression applies not, and and or when it contains several of them. The Boolean operators have an order of operations just like the math operators do: after any math and comparison operators evaluate, Python evaluates the not operators first, then the and operators, and then the or operators (Sweigart, 2025). The reference documentation lists the same order from the lowest priority to the highest as or, and, not (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Precedence makes an expression mean exactly one thing. Without it, a line that mixes and with or could be read as joining its parts in either order, and the two readings can give different answers. Chapter 1 introduced the idea for arithmetic; this section extends it to truth values.
Every compound condition that mixes the three operators depends on it, and so does every condition that combines comparisons with them, because comparisons are evaluated before the Boolean operators.

In True or False and False the operator and is applied first, giving False, and then or gives True, so the expression evaluates to True. Parentheses change the order: (True or False) and False evaluates to False. The operator not binds more tightly than and, so not True and False is read as (not True) and False and evaluates to False, whereas not (True and False) evaluates to True.

Do not rely on memory for a line that matters. A reader who has forgotten the order can read the line wrongly, and a parenthesis costs nothing. The common error is to expect that and and or are applied from left to right with equal weight, which would give a different answer for the first example above.

nodes.definition: After arithmetic and comparison operators, not is applied first, then and, then or.

nodes.label: Flow control
nodes.body: Flow control is the part of a program that decides which instructions run, in what order and how often. The textbook puts it plainly: based on how expressions evaluate, a program can decide to skip instructions, repeat them, or choose one of several instructions to run, and flow control statements decide which Python instructions to execute under which conditions (Sweigart, 2025). This chapter treats the first of these abilities, choosing; repeating instructions, which is done with loops (statements that run a block again and again), is the subject of the next chapter.

paras.text: Flow control is the part of a program that decides which instructions run, in what order and how often. The textbook puts it plainly: based on how expressions evaluate, a program can decide to skip instructions, repeat them, or choose one of several instructions to run, and flow control statements decide which Python instructions to execute under which conditions (Sweigart, 2025). This chapter treats the first of these abilities, choosing; repeating instructions, which is done with loops (statements that run a block again and again), is the subject of the next chapter.

A program that ran every line from the first to the last, in order, every time, could never react to its input. The textbook observes that you almost never want your programs to start from the first line of code and simply execute every line, straight to the end (Sweigart, 2025). Flow control is what turns a list of instructions into a program that responds to its data.

Flow control appears in every program of more than a few lines. Checking a password, sorting out which message to show, refusing invalid input and handling the several cases of a command all use the statements of this branch. The textbook illustrates them with flowcharts, in which the branching points are drawn as diamonds, so that the statement and the picture can be compared (Sweigart, 2025).

A flow control statement usually has a condition, which is an expression that Python tests for truth, and a block of indented lines that it runs or skips. The branch therefore first explains how statements are executed and how a flowchart shows the path of execution. It then explains the parts of a flow control statement, namely the condition, the block, the indentation that marks the block, the clause and the keyword that opens it. After that come the if, elif and else statements and the chain they form, and last the two expression forms that bring a choice or a name into a single expression.

The central mistake in this branch is to confuse a line that is written with a line that is executed. A line inside a block that is skipped never runs, so an error in it is not seen, and a line that is outdented by one level may run when the author thought it was skipped. Reading a program means following the path that its data takes through the conditions.

nodes.label: Execution flow
nodes.body: Execution flow is the path that execution takes through a program: which statement runs first, which runs next and which are skipped. Three ideas belong to it. A statement is the unit that is executed, program execution is the name for the instruction that is being executed at a given moment, and a flowchart is a diagram that draws the possible paths (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Execution flow is the path that execution takes through a program: which statement runs first, which runs next and which are skipped. Three ideas belong to it. A statement is the unit that is executed, program execution is the name for the instruction that is being executed at a given moment, and a flowchart is a diagram that draws the possible paths (Sweigart, 2025).

These three ideas give a learner the vocabulary for reasoning about a program before running it. Predicting what a program will print means following its execution, and explaining what went wrong means finding the point at which execution took a different path from the one that was intended.

The branch starts with the statement, the building block that the rest of the chapter specialises into flow control statements. It continues with program execution, which the textbook explains with the picture of a finger moving down the screen, and it ends with the flowchart, which turns that finger's path into a drawing.

The vocabulary pays for itself the first time a program appears to do nothing. A statement is executed for its effect, so a line that reads spam == 42 on its own is a complete and legal program that computes a Boolean and throws it away, while spam = 42 binds a name. Python also compiles a whole file before running any of it, which is why a syntax error on the last line stops the first line from printing at all (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Only after that does execution follow the path a flowchart draws, one statement at a time.

nodes.label: Flow control statement
nodes.body: A statement is the unit of a program that Python executes. The glossary defines it as part of a suite, a block of code, and as either an expression or one of several constructs with a keyword, such as if, while or for (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A flow control statement is a statement of the second kind: it does not compute a value for use elsewhere, but decides which other statements run (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A statement is the unit of a program that Python executes. The glossary defines it as part of a suite, a block of code, and as either an expression or one of several constructs with a keyword, such as if, while or for (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A flow control statement is a statement of the second kind: it does not compute a value for use elsewhere, but decides which other statements run (Sweigart, 2025).

The distinction between an expression and a statement explains what a line can be used for. An expression has a value and can be printed, stored or combined with others. A statement does something, and the glossary notes that some constructs are statements which cannot be used as expressions: it names while as an example and adds that assignments are statements, not expressions (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The if statement, with its elif and else parts, is the flow control statement of this chapter, and the next chapter adds the loop statements while and for. All of them are compound statements, which the reference documentation describes as statements that contain groups of other statements and affect or control how those statements are executed (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A compound statement consists of one or more clauses, and each clause consists of a header and a suite, which is the group of statements that the clause controls (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The headers of one compound statement stand at the same indentation level, and the textbook says the same in its own words: flow control statements often start with a condition and are always followed by a block of code (Sweigart, 2025).

A statement produces no value to print or store. Python makes the boundary visible: an assignment such as spam = 42 does not show a result in the interactive shell, whereas the expression spam does. When a decision has to produce a value inside a larger expression, the statement is the wrong tool and the conditional expression described later in this chapter is the right one.

nodes.definition: A statement that decides which instructions run next, such as if, elif and else.

nodes.label: Program execution
nodes.body: Program execution, or simply execution, is a term for the current instruction being executed (Sweigart, 2025). It is not a property of the text of a program but of a particular run: the same program can follow different paths on different occasions. The interpreter of Chapter 1 is the program that carries out the execution.

paras.text: Program execution, or simply execution, is a term for the current instruction being executed (Sweigart, 2025). It is not a property of the text of a program but of a particular run: the same program can follow different paths on different occasions. The interpreter of Chapter 1 is the program that carries out the execution.

The idea separates what is written from what happens. A reader who can say which line is being executed, and why the next one follows, can find a bug without running anything. The textbook offers a physical picture for it: if you put your finger on each line on your screen as the line is executed, you can think of your finger as the program execution (Sweigart, 2025).

In the hello.py program of Chapter 1, Python started executing instructions at the top and went down, one after another (Sweigart, 2025). Every program in this chapter starts that way too, but as soon as it contains a flow control statement the finger may jump over a block or choose between two.

Without flow control, execution moves straight down the program. With flow control statements, the textbook says, the finger will jump to different places in the source code based on conditions (Sweigart, 2025). In a program that sets age = 70 and then has an if statement that prints a message only when age > 65 holds, the line inside the block runs for this age, and it would be skipped for the age 20.

A line that is never executed is never checked for the errors that appear while a program runs. A program that contains if False: followed by a block that adds a number to a string, and then a print of the word done, runs without any error, because the faulty line is not reached. A syntax error is different: the parser finds it when it reads the program text, so a mistake in the shape of a skipped line is still reported, and nothing of the program runs.

nodes.example: the finger on the current line
nodes.definition: Program execution is the instruction that is being executed at a given moment; with flow control it jumps around the program.

nodes.label: Flowchart
nodes.body: A flowchart is a diagram of the steps of a process and the decisions between them. The textbook states that flow control statements directly correspond to the symbols in a flowchart, and it draws a flowchart for every statement that it introduces (Sweigart, 2025). Branching points are drawn as diamonds, the other steps as rectangles, and the starting and ending steps as rounded rectangles.

paras.text: A flowchart is a diagram of the steps of a process and the decisions between them. The textbook states that flow control statements directly correspond to the symbols in a flowchart, and it draws a flowchart for every statement that it introduces (Sweigart, 2025). Branching points are drawn as diamonds, the other steps as rectangles, and the starting and ending steps as rounded rectangles.

A flowchart shows all paths at once, which the text of a program does not. In a flowchart there is usually more than one way to go from the start to the end, and the same is true for the lines of a program (Sweigart, 2025). Drawing the paths is a way to plan a decision before writing it, and to check afterwards that every path leads somewhere sensible.

The chapter opens with a flowchart of what to do if it is raining, which a reader follows along the arrows from Start to End. Figures 2-2 to 2-7 then give a flowchart for the if statement, the else statement, the elif statement and the programs vampire.py, vampire2.py and littleKid.py (Sweigart, 2025).
