Each diamond stands for a condition, and the arrows leaving it lead to the steps that follow when the condition is true or false. Following the arrows from the start to the end reproduces the path that execution takes. Once the statements are written as code, the diamonds become the if and elif statements and the rectangles become their blocks.

A flowchart can reveal a bug that the code hides. The flowchart of the program vampire2.py in the textbook has a path that will logically never happen, because a person older than 2000 is already older than 100 and the first of those two tests catches them; the figure caption says so (Sweigart, 2025). A branch that can never be taken is a signal that the conditions are in the wrong order.

nodes.example: the flowchart of an if statement
nodes.definition: A diagram of a program's decisions: diamonds for branching points, rectangles for steps and rounded rectangles for the start and the end.

nodes.label: Control structure
nodes.body: A control structure is the set of parts out of which a flow control statement is built. A statement of this kind starts with a keyword and a condition, ends its first line with a colon, and is followed by a block of indented lines, which is called its clause (Sweigart, 2025). This branch names those parts: the condition, the block, the indentation that marks the block, the clause and the keyword.

paras.text: A control structure is the set of parts out of which a flow control statement is built. A statement of this kind starts with a keyword and a condition, ends its first line with a colon, and is followed by a block of indented lines, which is called its clause (Sweigart, 2025). This branch names those parts: the condition, the block, the indentation that marks the block, the clause and the keyword.

Learning the parts first makes every statement that follows easy to read. If, elif and else differ in the keyword and in whether they have a condition, but they share the shape of header, colon and indented block, and the same shape returns in the loops and function definitions of later chapters.

The five sections of the branch follow the order in which a reader meets the parts on the page: the condition that Python tests, the block that it controls, the indentation that Python reads to find the block, the clause that is the header and block together, and the keyword that opens the clause.

Because Python reads the indentation, the layout is part of the grammar and not a matter of taste. A line indented more deeply than the block it joins is refused with IndentationError: unexpected indent, and a tab mixed with spaces inside one block raises TabError: inconsistent use of tabs and spaces in indentation, since the interpreter cannot then tell which lines belong together (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The style guide settles the amount at four spaces for each level, which is how every block in this chapter is written (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

nodes.label: Condition
nodes.body: A condition is an expression that a flow control statement evaluates to decide what to do. The textbook explains that the Boolean expressions seen so far could all be considered conditions, which are the same thing as expressions; condition is just a more specific name in the context of flow control statements (Sweigart, 2025). An if statement, for example, executes its block when its condition is true and skips it when its condition is false.

paras.text: A condition is an expression that a flow control statement evaluates to decide what to do. The textbook explains that the Boolean expressions seen so far could all be considered conditions, which are the same thing as expressions; condition is just a more specific name in the context of flow control statements (Sweigart, 2025). An if statement, for example, executes its block when its condition is true and skips it when its condition is false.

Almost every flow control statement uses a condition, so a condition is how a program connects its data to its decisions (Sweigart, 2025). The textbook gives two ways to say it in English: if this condition is true, do this thing, or else do this other thing; and keep repeating these instructions as long as this condition continues to be true.

A condition follows the word if or elif, as in name == 'Alice' or age < 12. The textbook also uses conditions that combine several comparisons, such as unit == 'TB' or unit == 'tb'. The second form of the English sentence, repeating while a condition holds, belongs to the loop statements of the next chapter.

Python evaluates the condition and reads the result as true or false. The reference documentation says that the if statement selects exactly one of its suites by evaluating the expressions one by one until one is found to be true (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook says that a condition always evaluates to a Boolean value, and that is the usual case, but Python accepts any value and applies the rule of truthiness, so a line such as if name: is legal.

A condition is an expression, not a statement. An assignment cannot take its place, and the slip of writing one equals sign instead of two in the condition of an if statement is reported as a syntax error. Spelling the condition out more than necessary is also a mistake of style: the style guide advises against comparing a Boolean value with True or False using ==, so if greeting: is preferred to if greeting == True: (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

nodes.definition: A condition is an expression evaluated for truth to decide which block runs.

nodes.label: Block
nodes.body: A block is a group of lines of code that are treated together. The textbook explains that lines of Python code can be grouped together in blocks, and that you can tell when a block begins and ends from the indentation of the lines of code (Sweigart, 2025). The reference documentation calls such a group a suite, a group of statements controlled by a clause (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A block is a group of lines of code that are treated together. The textbook explains that lines of Python code can be grouped together in blocks, and that you can tell when a block begins and ends from the indentation of the lines of code (Sweigart, 2025). The reference documentation calls such a group a suite, a group of statements controlled by a clause (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A block decides what belongs to a decision. Everything that is part of the block runs together when the condition holds, and everything that is outside it runs regardless. Because Python marks blocks by indentation, the layout that a human reads and the structure that the interpreter reads are one and the same, so a program cannot look as if it did one thing while doing another.

A block follows every flow control statement of this chapter: the lines after if, after elif and after else. The textbook points out that blocks can be found inside other blocks, and that this chapter uses blocks only with if, elif and else, although several other statements use blocks as well (Sweigart, 2025).

The textbook gives four rules for blocks. A new block begins when the indentation increases. Blocks can contain other blocks. A block ends when the indentation decreases to zero or to a containing block's indentation. And Python expects a new block immediately after any statement that ends with a colon (Sweigart, 2025). In its example the first block is the line print('Hello, Mary'), which contains the lines after it, including an inner block with the single line print('Access granted.') and another with print('Wrong password.').

One level of indentation decides whether a line is part of a block. In a program that prints big inside the block of if x > 3: and then prints always, the second line is part of the block when it is indented and runs every time when it is not. An error in the indentation does not look like an error to a reader, so the structure of the blocks is the first thing to check when a program behaves strangely.

nodes.definition: A block is a group of lines at the same indentation; Python uses indentation, not braces, to mark it.

nodes.label: Indentation
nodes.body: Indentation is the whitespace at the beginning of a line of code. The language reference says that leading whitespace at the beginning of a logical line (one statement, even when it is written over several physical lines) is used to compute the indentation level of the line, which in turn is used to determine the grouping of statements (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In Python it is part of the syntax, not decoration.

paras.text: Indentation is the whitespace at the beginning of a line of code. The language reference says that leading whitespace at the beginning of a logical line (one statement, even when it is written over several physical lines) is used to compute the indentation level of the line, which in turn is used to determine the grouping of statements (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In Python it is part of the syntax, not decoration.

Many languages mark blocks with braces and treat the layout as a matter of taste. Python lets the layout carry the meaning, so that a program that looks right is right about its structure. The textbook adds the sentence that Python uses indentation to create blocks of code, and the language reference gives the exact procedure (Sweigart, 2025).

Every flow control statement is followed by indented lines, and a statement nested inside a block (placed inside it, as a part of it) is indented one level further, as in the textbook's example of an if statement inside another if statement (Sweigart, 2025).

To read the indentation, Python splits the text of a program into tokens, the smallest units of the text such as names, numbers, operators and line ends. It keeps a stack of indentation levels, a list in which only the last entry is looked at and changed, starting with a single zero. At the beginning of each logical line it compares the indentation of the line with the top of the stack. If the two are equal, nothing happens. If the line is indented more, the new level is pushed and an INDENT token is produced, which opens a block. If the line is indented less, the level must be one that is on the stack, and each larger level that is removed produces a DEDENT token, which closes a block (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Wrong indentation is reported as an IndentationError, a kind of SyntaxError. A block that is missing after a colon gives expected an indented block after 'if' statement on line 1; a line that is indented for no reason gives unexpected indent; and a line that returns to a level that does not exist gives unindent does not match any outer indentation level. Mixing tabs and spaces in the same file can also cause an error, and a TabError is raised when the meaning would depend on the width of a tab (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.example: four spaces in front of a line
nodes.definition: Indentation is the whitespace at the start of a line; Python compares it between lines to find which lines form a block.

nodes.label: Clause
nodes.body: A clause is one part of a compound statement. In the textbook's wording, flow control statements are always followed by a block of code called the clause; the block after an if statement is the if clause, and the block after else is the else clause (Sweigart, 2025). The reference documentation uses the word for the header and its suite together: a compound statement consists of one or more clauses, and a clause consists of a header and a suite (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A clause is one part of a compound statement. In the textbook's wording, flow control statements are always followed by a block of code called the clause; the block after an if statement is the if clause, and the block after else is the else clause (Sweigart, 2025). The reference documentation uses the word for the header and its suite together: a compound statement consists of one or more clauses, and a clause consists of a header and a suite (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The word lets a learner talk about a single branch of an if chain without mixing it up with the whole statement. Two usages exist, and both are common: the textbook calls the controlled block the clause, whereas the reference calls the header with its block a clause. Knowing both prevents misunderstanding when one source is read after the other.

An if statement has an if clause, possibly followed by elif clauses and an else clause. In the reference documentation each clause header begins with a uniquely identifying keyword and ends with a colon, and the headers of one compound statement stand at the same indentation level (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The suite of a clause can be written in two ways: as one or more indented statements on the following lines, which is the form the textbook teaches, or as simple statements on the same line as the header. Only the indented form can contain nested compound statements (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The style guide discourages putting the suite on the header's line, and it says never to do so for clauses of multi-clause statements (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

The colon at the end of the header is required. Without it Python reports a SyntaxError with the message expected ':' for a line such as if True. After the colon the next line must be indented, or the IndentationError described under indentation is raised.

nodes.definition: A clause is a header that begins with a keyword and ends with a colon, together with the block of statements it controls.

nodes.label: Keyword
nodes.body: A keyword is a word that the language reserves for its own use. The language reference states that keywords cannot be used as ordinary identifiers, and that they must be spelled exactly as written; its list includes False, None, True, and, or, not, if, elif and else (Python Software Foundation, 2026). They are what a reader sees at the start of a flow control statement.

paras.text: A keyword is a word that the language reserves for its own use. The language reference states that keywords cannot be used as ordinary identifiers, and that they must be spelled exactly as written; its list includes False, None, True, and, or, not, if, elif and else (Python Software Foundation, 2026). They are what a reader sees at the start of a flow control statement.

Keywords tell the interpreter what kind of statement a line is. The word if starts a decision and the word else starts its alternative. Because the words are reserved, a program cannot give them a second meaning: the assignment of a value to True is illegal for this reason.

The if, elif and else of this chapter are keywords, and so are True, False, None, and, or and not. The standard library offers a module named keyword that can test a word: keyword.iskeyword('if') evaluates to True, and keyword.iskeyword('true') evaluates to False because the lowercase spelling is not reserved (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Python recognises keywords when it reads the program text. Every keyword is written in lowercase except False, None and True, which begin with a capital letter. A few words are reserved only in some contexts; these soft keywords are explained in the section on the match statement, where match and case are the examples.

A keyword cannot be used as the name of a variable. The line if = 3 is rejected with a SyntaxError whose message is invalid syntax. Beginners meet this when they choose natural names, and the remedy is to pick another name. A word that merely looks like a keyword, such as the lowercase true, is not reserved and is reported as an unknown name instead.

nodes.example: the words if, else and True
nodes.definition: A keyword is a word reserved by the language; it has a fixed meaning and cannot be used as an ordinary name.

nodes.label: Branching
nodes.body: Branching is the choice between alternative blocks of code. In Python it is done with the if statement and with the elif and else clauses that may follow it. The textbook describes the most common flow control statement as the if statement and the others as additions to it (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Branching is the choice between alternative blocks of code. In Python it is done with the if statement and with the elif and else clauses that may follow it. The textbook describes the most common flow control statement as the if statement and the others as additions to it (Sweigart, 2025).

Branching is what makes a program respond to its input. Each additional clause adds an alternative, and the reader of a program can see the alternatives one below the other. The tutorial notes that an if, elif and else sequence is a substitute for the switch or case statements found in other languages (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The branch takes the if statement first, then the elif clause that adds a further condition, then the else clause that handles everything that is left, and finally the chain that the three form together and the rules for putting them in order.

Exactly one clause of a chain runs, and it is the first whose condition is true. In a chain that tests age < 12 and then age < 20, an age of 10 takes the first clause and the second is never reached, so exchanging the two conditions changes the answer for every age under twelve (Sweigart, 2025). A chain with no else clause may run none of its blocks at all, which is the usual cause of the unassigned name that the decision patterns of this chapter meet later.

nodes.label: If statement
nodes.body: The if statement is the most common flow control statement. Its block, the if clause, executes when the condition of the statement is True, and the block is skipped when the condition is False (Sweigart, 2025). In Python an if statement consists of the if keyword, a condition, a colon and, starting on the next line, an indented block of code (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The if statement is the most common flow control statement. Its block, the if clause, executes when the condition of the statement is True, and the block is skipped when the condition is False (Sweigart, 2025). In Python an if statement consists of the if keyword, a condition, a colon and, starting on the next line, an indented block of code (Sweigart, 2025).

The statement lets a program do something only in the cases in which it is meant. Checking whether a person's name is Alice, whether a number is large enough, or whether a file was found are each one if statement. All other branching builds on it, since elif and else clauses are additions to an if.

The textbook's example checks a name: with name = 'Alice' and the statement if name == 'Alice': followed by an indented print('Hi, Alice.'), the program prints Hi, Alice. When the variable holds another string, the message does not appear because the block is skipped (Sweigart, 2025).

Python evaluates the condition and reads its value as true or false. If it is true, the indented block runs and execution then continues with the first line after the block; if it is false, the block is skipped. The reference documentation puts it as selecting exactly one of the suites by evaluating the expressions one by one until one is found to be true, after which no other part of the statement is executed or evaluated (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The three details that cause most errors are the colon after the condition, the indentation of the block and the comparison operator in the condition. A missing colon is reported as a SyntaxError, a missing block as an IndentationError, and a single equals sign in the condition as a SyntaxError that suggests ==. The block is skipped without any message when the condition is false, so a program that prints nothing is not necessarily broken.

nodes.definition: if runs its block only when its condition is true.

nodes.label: Elif clause
nodes.body: The elif clause is an else-if clause. It always follows an if statement or another elif clause, and it provides another condition that is checked only if all of the previous conditions were False (Sweigart, 2025). Like the if statement it consists of a keyword, a condition, a colon and an indented block of code (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The elif clause is an else-if clause. It always follows an if statement or another elif clause, and it provides another condition that is checked only if all of the previous conditions were False (Sweigart, 2025). Like the if statement it consists of a keyword, a condition, a colon and an indented block of code (Sweigart, 2025).

Use if or else when only one of two clauses should run. Use elif when one of many possible clauses should run, as when several age groups each get a different message. The tutorial says that the keyword elif is short for else if and is useful to avoid excessive indentation (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The textbook adds an elif to its name checker so that a person younger than twelve receives another greeting, and then adds two more for ages above 2000 and above 100. With name = 'Carol' and age = 3000 the chain prints the sentence Unlike you, Alice is not an undead, immortal vampire (Sweigart, 2025).

Python tests the conditions from top to bottom. The elif clause runs if its condition is True and every earlier condition was False. Once one condition is found to be True, the rest of the elif clauses are automatically skipped, and when all conditions are False Python skips all of the clauses (Sweigart, 2025). In a chain of elif statements only one or none of the clauses will be executed.

The order of the elif clauses matters. If the test age > 100 is written before the test age > 2000, a person aged 3000 satisfies the first one and the second can never be reached: the program prints You are not Alice, grannie. The textbook calls this a bug that is introduced by rearranging the clauses (Sweigart, 2025). Put the more specific condition before the more general one.

nodes.definition: elif tests a further condition only when every earlier one was false; at most one branch runs.

nodes.label: Else clause
nodes.body: The else clause is the part of an if statement that runs when nothing else has. An if clause can optionally be followed by an else statement, and the else clause is executed only when the condition of the if statement is False (Sweigart, 2025). Unlike if and elif, an else statement has no condition: it consists of the keyword else, a colon and an indented block.

paras.text: The else clause is the part of an if statement that runs when nothing else has. An if clause can optionally be followed by an else statement, and the else clause is executed only when the condition of the if statement is False (Sweigart, 2025). Unlike if and elif, an else statement has no condition: it consists of the keyword else, a colon and an indented block.

The else clause makes sure that every case is handled. Without it a chain of conditions can end without doing anything, and the program carries on as if a decision had been made. With it the programmer states what happens in all other cases, which is often an error message.

In the textbook's name checker, the else clause offers a different greeting if the person's name is not Alice: the program prints Hello, stranger. For a person named Carol aged 3000, with an if, an elif for ages below twelve and an else clause, it prints the sentence You are neither Alice nor a little kid (Sweigart, 2025).

The reference documentation says that if all expressions are false, the suite of the else clause, if present, is executed (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook draws the consequence for chains: with an else after the last elif, it is guaranteed that at least one, and only one, of the clauses will be executed (Sweigart, 2025).

The else clause must come last. Python 3.14 reports an elif that follows an else with the message 'elif' block follows an 'else' block, whereas Python 3.12 says only invalid syntax. An else clause has no condition of its own, so it cannot test anything: a line such as else x > 3: is a SyntaxError with the message invalid syntax.

nodes.definition: else runs its block when no earlier condition in the chain was true.

nodes.label: Branch chain
nodes.body: A branch chain is an if statement together with the elif clauses and the else clause that follow it. The textbook states two rules for putting them together: there is always exactly one if statement, with any elif statements following it, and if you want to be sure that at least one clause is executed, you close the structure with an else statement (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A branch chain is an if statement together with the elif clauses and the else clause that follow it. The textbook states two rules for putting them together: there is always exactly one if statement, with any elif statements following it, and if you want to be sure that at least one clause is executed, you close the structure with an else statement (Sweigart, 2025).

The chain expresses a decision with many outcomes in a way that guarantees there is only one result. In plain English, the textbook says, it means: if the first condition is true, do this; else, if the second condition is true, do that; otherwise, do something else (Sweigart, 2025). Chaining is cleaner than a series of nested decisions, and it states the order of the tests.

A ticket price that depends on age is a typical chain: one clause for children, one for adults and a closing else clause for seniors. Any classification of a value into ranges, or a command that can be one of several words, has the same shape.

Python tests the conditions in the order written and runs the block of the first one that is true; it does not evaluate the later conditions (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A chain is different from a sequence of separate if statements. With age = 70, two separate statements testing age > 12 and age > 65 both run and print A and B, whereas the same tests joined by elif print only A.

Overlapping conditions make the order important, so a chain should be read from the top. A chain without else may run no block, which the textbook states as only one or none of the clauses will be executed (Sweigart, 2025). When a variable is assigned in the blocks of a chain, a missing else can leave it unassigned, a bug that the worked programs of this chapter demonstrate.

nodes.definition: A chain of if, elif and else clauses runs at most one block, and exactly one when it ends with else.

nodes.label: Expression form
nodes.body: An expression form is a construct that brings a choice or a naming into a single expression, so that it has a value and can be used inside larger expressions. The chapter has two: the conditional expression, which chooses between two values, and the assignment expression, which gives a name to a value while it is being used. Both are described in the language reference as expressions, in contrast with the statements of the previous branches (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: An expression form is a construct that brings a choice or a naming into a single expression, so that it has a value and can be used inside larger expressions. The chapter has two: the conditional expression, which chooses between two values, and the assignment expression, which gives a name to a value while it is being used. Both are described in the language reference as expressions, in contrast with the statements of the previous branches (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A statement cannot be placed inside a larger expression, but a choice sometimes has to be. A message that depends on a condition may be needed as an argument of a function, or a value may be needed twice in one condition. The two forms of this branch make that possible without splitting the line into several statements.

The conditional expression is the older and more common of the two. The assignment expression arrived in Python 3.8 and appears mostly in conditions. Both are used sparingly, because a long expression is harder to read than the statements it replaces.

Both forms are expressions, so both have a value that can be used on the spot. The conditional expression 'child' if age < 12 else 'adult' evaluates to 'child' for an age of 10 and can be passed straight to print, where an if statement could not (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The assignment expression both names and yields: the condition (n := len('Alice')) > 3 evaluates to True and leaves n bound to 5, so the length is computed once and is still available inside the block.

nodes.label: Conditional expression
nodes.body: A conditional expression, sometimes called a ternary operator because it combines three operands, is an alternative to the if-else statement. Because it is an expression, it returns a value and can appear as a sub-expression (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It is written x if C else y, where C is a condition and x and y are the two possible values.

paras.text: A conditional expression, sometimes called a ternary operator because it combines three operands, is an alternative to the if-else statement. Because it is an expression, it returns a value and can appear as a sub-expression (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It is written x if C else y, where C is a condition and x and y are the two possible values.

Choosing between two values is so common that a statement of four lines is out of proportion. A conditional expression keeps the choice on the line where the value is needed, for example in an assignment or inside a call. It also shows clearly that the whole construct produces one value.

A typical use gives a variable one of two values: 'even' if 10 % 2 == 0 else 'odd' evaluates to 'even', and with 7 in place of 10 it evaluates to 'odd'. It is the right form when both branches are simple values and the choice is small.

Python first evaluates the condition C, not x. If C is true, x is evaluated and its value is returned; otherwise y is evaluated and its value is returned (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Only one of the two values is evaluated, so 'adult' if 20 >= 18 else 1 / 0 evaluates to 'adult' without dividing by zero. In the precedence table the conditional expression comes near the bottom, below the Boolean operators, so a condition does not need parentheses.

The conditional expression is not a replacement for the if statement. It chooses values, not actions, so each part must be an expression; Python 3.14 reports a statement such as pass in place of a value with the message expected expression after 'else', but statement is given, where Python 3.12 says only invalid syntax (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Nesting several conditional expressions quickly becomes unreadable, and then a normal if statement is clearer.

nodes.definition: x if C else y chooses between two values in a single expression.

nodes.label: Assignment expression
nodes.body: An assignment expression, also called a named expression or, informally, the walrus operator (the symbol := looks like the eyes and tusks of a walrus), assigns an expression to an identifier while also returning the value of the expression (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It is written with the operator :=. It was added in Python 3.8 by PEP 572, whose formal name for the construct is assignment expressions (Angelico et al., 2018).

paras.text: An assignment expression, also called a named expression or, informally, the walrus operator (the symbol := looks like the eyes and tusks of a walrus), assigns an expression to an identifier while also returning the value of the expression (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It is written with the operator :=. It was added in Python 3.8 by PEP 572, whose formal name for the construct is assignment expressions (Angelico et al., 2018).

Naming the result of an expression is an important part of programming, because it allows a descriptive name to be used in place of a longer expression and permits reuse (Angelico et al., 2018). Until the new form existed, naming a value required a separate assignment statement and was impossible inside a condition.

The reference documentation shows it in the conditions of if and while statements, where a value is computed, tested and then kept for use inside the block (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A small case in this chapter's terms is a condition that needs a length twice: the line if (size := len(name)) > 3: tests the length and also keeps it in the name size for the block.

The expression (limit := 10) > 5 assigns 10 to limit and then compares the value with 5, so it evaluates to True and limit remains available afterwards. With name = 'Alice', the statement if (size := len(name)) > 3: followed by print(size) prints 5. The reference documentation says that assignment expressions must be surrounded by parentheses when used as expression statements and in several other places, but that parentheses are not required in if and while statements (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The operator := is not a second form of =. As a statement on its own, x := 3 is rejected with the message invalid syntax, and the plain assignment statement is the right tool for naming a value on a line of its own. Overusing the form makes conditions harder to read, so it is best kept for places where the value is needed immediately.

nodes.definition: An assignment expression, written name := value, assigns the value to the name and also yields it.

nodes.label: Modern practice
nodes.body: Modern practice is the way Python programmers work today: the constructs that current Python offers beyond the textbook and the conventions that experienced developers follow when they write conditions. An advanced course teaches this practice next to the basics of the book, so that students do not have to unlearn habits later.

paras.text: Modern practice is the way Python programmers work today: the constructs that current Python offers beyond the textbook and the conventions that experienced developers follow when they write conditions. An advanced course teaches this practice next to the basics of the book, so that students do not have to unlearn habits later.

The textbook teaches decisions with if, elif and else, and that is complete enough for every program of its chapter. Python 3.10 nevertheless added a statement for choosing among patterns, and the official style guide has firm views on how conditions should be written. A student who knows only the book writes code that works but looks dated to other programmers.

The match statement is met in code written for Python 3.10 or later, in the documentation and in the release notes. The style guide, PEP 8, is a process document whose status is Active, and it is the reference to turn to whenever a programmer asks how a piece of Python should be written (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

Two branches follow. Pattern matching explains the match statement and its parts: the case patterns, the wildcard, sequence patterns, guards and the soft keywords that make the new statement possible. Style collects the recommendations of PEP 8 that concern the ideas of this chapter, namely how to compare Boolean values and singletons, how to test for emptiness and how to indent.

Modern practice does not replace the basics. A match statement is not a better if statement; it is a different tool for a particular shape of problem, and a style recommendation is a convention that a team may adapt. The advice of this branch is therefore given with the reasons that the sources give for it.

nodes.label: Pattern matching
nodes.body: Pattern matching is a way of choosing between alternatives by comparing a value with patterns that describe its shape. Python 3.10 added it as the match statement, specified in PEP 634 and explained for learners in PEP 636 (Bucher and van Rossum, 2020) (Moisset, 2020). A pattern can be a plain value, but it can also describe a sequence of a given length, and it can capture parts of the value into names.

paras.text: Pattern matching is a way of choosing between alternatives by comparing a value with patterns that describe its shape. Python 3.10 added it as the match statement, specified in PEP 634 and explained for learners in PEP 636 (Bucher and van Rossum, 2020) (Moisset, 2020). A pattern can be a plain value, but it can also describe a sequence of a given length, and it can capture parts of the value into names.

A long elif chain that compares one value with many constants is repetitive: the value is named in every condition. A match statement names it once and lists the cases below it. The tutorial recommends the statement when the same value is compared with several constants, or when specific types are checked (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The sections of this branch go from the whole to the parts. The match statement shows the structure and the order in which the cases are tried. The case pattern, wildcard pattern and sequence pattern describe the three kinds of pattern that suffice for commands and status codes. The guard adds a condition to a pattern, and the soft keyword explains why match and case can be new words without breaking old programs.

The cases are tried from the top, and the first pattern that fits wins, so a case of the wildcard at the end catches everything left over (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A pattern binds as well as tests: matching the value [1, 2] against a sequence pattern of two names leaves the first bound to 1 and the second to 2, which is how one pattern replaces a length test and two index expressions. A value that no case matches simply falls through, so a match statement without a wildcard can do nothing at all and report nothing either.

nodes.label: Match statement
nodes.body: A match statement takes an expression and compares its value with successive patterns given as one or more case blocks. The tutorial says that this is superficially similar to a switch statement in C, Java or JavaScript, but more similar to pattern matching in languages like Rust or Haskell (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Only the first pattern that matches is executed, and if no case matches, none of the branches runs. The statement was added in Python 3.10 (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A match statement takes an expression and compares its value with successive patterns given as one or more case blocks. The tutorial says that this is superficially similar to a switch statement in C, Java or JavaScript, but more similar to pattern matching in languages like Rust or Haskell (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Only the first pattern that matches is executed, and if no case matches, none of the branches runs. The statement was added in Python 3.10 (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The statement is made for the situation in which one value, such as a command, a status code or a pair of coordinates, determines what happens next. PEP 636 motivates it with a text adventure in which the user types commands and the program must interpret them (Moisset, 2020). Written with elif, each case repeats the name of the value; written with match, the cases line up.

The tutorial's examples handle status codes, points and colours, and PEP 636 builds the command interpreter of a text adventure with it (Python Software Foundation, 2026) (Moisset, 2020). The Python documentation describes the statement in the language reference and in the tutorial, and the release notes of Python 3.10 announce it as PEP 634 (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The reference documentation describes the flow. The subject expression after match is evaluated once. Each pattern in a case block is then attempted against the subject value in order, and the first pattern that succeeds, and whose guard if any is true, has its block executed (Python Software Foundation, 2026). With command = 'quit' and the cases 'go', 'quit' and _, the program prints bye. Names that a successful pattern binds outlive the block and can be used after the match statement.

If no case matches and there is no wildcard, nothing happens and no error is raised: with the command 'dance' and a single case 'go', the program continues with the line after the statement. The statement also needs Python 3.10 or later. Finally, a bare name in a case is not a comparison but a capture, which the section on case patterns explains.

nodes.definition: Since Python 3.10 a match statement compares a value against successive case patterns, an alternative to a long elif chain.

nodes.label: Case pattern
nodes.body: A case pattern is the description that follows the word case. According to the reference documentation, pattern matching takes a pattern as input, following case, and a subject value, following match; the pattern, which may contain subpatterns (patterns inside a pattern), is matched against the subject value, and the outcome is a success or a failure and possibly the binding of matched values to names (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A case pattern is the description that follows the word case. According to the reference documentation, pattern matching takes a pattern as input, following case, and a subject value, following match; the pattern, which may contain subpatterns (patterns inside a pattern), is matched against the subject value, and the outcome is a success or a failure and possibly the binding of matched values to names (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Patterns are what make the statement more than a row of comparisons. A literal pattern checks a value, a capture pattern keeps a part of the value, and an OR pattern, written with vertical bars, accepts several alternatives in one case, so that related cases share a block.

The tutorial's example separates the status codes 400, 404 and 418, and groups 401, 403 and 404 with the pattern 401 | 403 | 404 (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In a program that sets status = 403 and matches it against the cases 400, 401 | 403 | 404 and _, the block of the second case runs and the program prints not allowed.

A literal pattern, a value written out in the code such as 401 or 'quit', succeeds when the subject is equal to the literal, except for None, True and False, which are compared with is (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A capture pattern is a name; it always succeeds and sets the name to the subject, which is called binding the name. An OR pattern tries its alternatives in turn and succeeds as soon as one does (Python Software Foundation, 2026). When a pattern succeeds, the names it bound outlive the executed block.

A name in a case is a capture and not a comparison. With expected = 'quit', command = 'go' and a single case expected:, the pattern succeeds anyway and sets expected to 'go', so the program prints matched go and has overwritten the variable. To compare with a stored constant, the tutorial says the constant must be a dotted name, such as Color.RED or math.pi, to keep it from being read as a capture variable (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.definition: A pattern after case describes the values it matches; it can be a literal, a name that captures the value, or alternatives joined by |.

nodes.label: Wildcard pattern
nodes.body: The wildcard pattern is written with a single underscore. The reference documentation says that a wildcard pattern always succeeds, matching anything, and binds no name (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The tutorial describes the underscore as a variable name that acts as a wildcard and never fails to match.

paras.text: The wildcard pattern is written with a single underscore. The reference documentation says that a wildcard pattern always succeeds, matching anything, and binds no name (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The tutorial describes the underscore as a variable name that acts as a wildcard and never fails to match.

A match statement does nothing when no case matches, which is rarely what a program wants for an unknown command. The wildcard provides the case for everything else, in the way that the else clause does in a chain of if and elif clauses.

The wildcard is the last case of the tutorial's status example, which returns a message for any status that the other cases do not know, and it closes the command example of this section: with the command 'dance' the program prints unknown.

A case block that cannot fail is called irrefutable. The reference allows at most one irrefutable case block in a match statement and requires it to be the last (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Python enforces the rule when it reads the program: a wildcard case followed by another case is rejected with the SyntaxError message wildcard makes remaining patterns unreachable, which means that the later cases could never be used.

The underscore is special only inside patterns. The reference says that it is a soft keyword within any pattern, but that outside patterns it is an identifier as usual (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A capture pattern with an ordinary name has the same effect of matching everything and, in addition, binds the name, so a name in the last position keeps the value that the wildcard throws away.

nodes.definition: The pattern _ matches anything and binds no name; as the last case it handles every value that no earlier case matched.

nodes.label: Sequence pattern
nodes.body: A sequence pattern describes a sequence by listing patterns for its items. The reference documentation states that it contains several subpatterns to be matched against sequence elements, and that the syntax is similar to the unpacking of a list or tuple, that is, the assignment of its items to several names in one statement; there is no difference whether parentheses or square brackets are used (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A sequence pattern describes a sequence by listing patterns for its items. The reference documentation states that it contains several subpatterns to be matched against sequence elements, and that the syntax is similar to the unpacking of a list or tuple, that is, the assignment of its items to several names in one statement; there is no difference whether parentheses or square brackets are used (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Commands usually arrive as a few words, and the program must know how many words it received before it can use them. PEP 636 starts from the observation that unpacking a command into an action and an object fails with an error if the user types more or fewer words than two (Moisset, 2020). A sequence pattern checks the length and takes the parts in one step.

The pattern is used for commands such as ['go', direction] and ['quit'], for coordinate pairs such as (x, y), and for any value that has a fixed shape. The tutorial notes that tuple and list patterns have exactly the same meaning and match arbitrary sequences, with the exception that they do not match strings (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

For a fixed-length pattern the subject must be a sequence of the same length, and the subpatterns are matched with the items from left to right, stopping at the first failure (Python Software Foundation, 2026). With command = ['go', 'north'], the case ['go', direction] succeeds, binds direction to 'north', and the program prints going north. A star subpattern such as *rest matches a list of the remaining items (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A string is not matched by a sequence pattern, even though a string is a sequence of characters. The reference says that if the subject is a string or a sequence of bytes the sequence pattern fails (Python Software Foundation, 2026): matching 'ab' against the case [a, b] fails, and a program with a wildcard case prints no match.

nodes.definition: A pattern that matches a sequence of a given length and binds names to its items.

nodes.label: Guard
nodes.body: A guard is an extra condition that is attached to a case. It takes the form of the word if followed by an expression, and the reference documentation says that it must succeed for the code inside the case block to execute (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A guard is an extra condition that is attached to a case. It takes the form of the word if followed by an expression, and the reference documentation says that it must succeed for the code inside the case block to execute (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Patterns can describe the shape and the constants of a value, but not every relationship between its parts. A guard supplies the rest, for example that the two coordinates of a point are equal, which a pattern alone cannot say.

The tutorial uses a guard to separate the points that lie on a diagonal from the others (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The same idea can be written for a pair: the case (x, y) if x == y selects the pair (3, 3), and the case (x, y) that follows it handles every other pair.

Python first checks the pattern. If it fails, the guard is not evaluated and the next case block is checked. If it succeeds, the names are bound and the guard is evaluated: a true guard selects the case block, a false guard does not, and the next case is tried (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The tutorial points out that value capture happens before the guard is evaluated (Python Software Foundation, 2026). For the pair (3, 3) the program prints on the diagonal at 3, and for (3, 4) it prints elsewhere.

A guard belongs to the case line and is not an if statement. If the guard raises an exception, it propagates, and guards are evaluated in order, one case at a time, until a case block is selected (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Do not rely on a guard to run, because a case whose pattern fails never reaches its guard.

nodes.definition: A guard is an if condition after a pattern; the case block is selected only when the pattern matches and the guard is true.

nodes.label: Soft keyword
nodes.body: A soft keyword is a name that is reserved only in specific contexts. The language reference lists match, case and _ as soft keywords when they are used in the match statement, and it adds that the distinction is made by the parser and not when the text is split into tokens (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A further soft keyword, type, belongs to a statement that this course does not use. The concept was added in Python 3.10 together with the match statement.

paras.text: A soft keyword is a name that is reserved only in specific contexts. The language reference lists match, case and _ as soft keywords when they are used in the match statement, and it adds that the distinction is made by the parser and not when the text is split into tokens (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A further soft keyword, type, belongs to a statement that this course does not use. The concept was added in Python 3.10 together with the match statement.

Soft keywords are a compatibility measure. As the reference puts it, they make it possible to extend the grammar while preserving compatibility with existing code that uses these names as identifier names (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Without them, adding the match statement would have broken every program that had a variable called match.

The standard library module keyword can tell the two kinds of word apart. The call keyword.iskeyword('match') evaluates to False, while keyword.issoftkeyword('match') evaluates to True, and keyword.iskeyword('if') evaluates to True (Python Software Foundation, 2026). PEP 634 explains that match and case are recognised as keywords when they are part of a match statement or a case block only (Bucher and van Rossum, 2020).

Outside a match statement the words are ordinary names. A program may assign match = 3 and case = 4 and then print match + case, which prints 7. Inside a match statement the parser reads the same words as keywords, so there is no clash between the two uses.

That a word is allowed as a name does not make it a good name. A reader who sees a variable called match in the neighbourhood of a match statement has to work out which meaning applies, so the names are best avoided even though Python permits them.

nodes.definition: A soft keyword is a word that acts as a keyword only in a particular context, so it can still be used as an ordinary name elsewhere.

nodes.label: Style
nodes.body: Style is the set of conventions for writing code that other people can read easily. For Python the main reference is PEP 8, the style guide for Python code, written by Guido van Rossum, Barry Warsaw and Alyssa Coghlan (Van Rossum et al., 2001). This branch collects the recommendations of PEP 8 that concern the ideas of Chapter 2.

paras.text: Style is the set of conventions for writing code that other people can read easily. For Python the main reference is PEP 8, the style guide for Python code, written by Guido van Rossum, Barry Warsaw and Alyssa Coghlan (Van Rossum et al., 2001). This branch collects the recommendations of PEP 8 that concern the ideas of Chapter 2.

PEP 8 recalls that code is read much more often than it is written (Van Rossum et al., 2001), and readers expect the conventions of their community. A condition written in the recommended way is shorter, and a reviewer can read it without stopping. Style recommendations are also not arbitrary: several of them protect against genuine mistakes, such as the comparison of a value with None.

Four sections follow. The recommendation on Boolean comparison says how to test a Boolean value, the one on singleton comparison says how to test for None, the one on emptiness says how to test a sequence, and the one on indentation says how to lay out blocks. The sections quote PEP 8 and test its claims with short programs.

The recommendations can be tested instead of being taken on authority. For a real Boolean the condition greeting == True and the plain condition greeting agree, since True == True and False == True give the value back unchanged; for every other value they part company, because bool('False') is True while 'False' == True is False (Van Rossum et al., 2001). The same guide asks that a comparison with None use is or is not rather than the equality operators, and that an empty sequence be tested with not before the name rather than by comparing its length with zero.

nodes.label: Boolean comparison style
nodes.body: PEP 8 recommends that a Boolean value not be compared to True or False with the equality operator. Its example reads: correct is if greeting:, wrong is if greeting == True:, and the form if greeting is True: is called worse (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

paras.text: PEP 8 recommends that a Boolean value not be compared to True or False with the equality operator. Its example reads: correct is if greeting:, wrong is if greeting == True:, and the form if greeting is True: is called worse (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

A condition is already a truth value, so comparing it with True adds a comparison without adding information. The longer form is also less safe, because it tests something different from what its author usually means: with greeting = 'hello', the condition greeting == True is false, because the string is not equal to True, while the condition greeting is true, because a non-empty string counts as true.

The textbook's own Opposite Day program contains conditions such as if today_is_opposite_day == True: (Sweigart, 2025). The program is correct, and a reviewer who follows PEP 8 would write if today_is_opposite_day: instead. The same applies to conditions that come out of comparisons: they can be used as they are.

The comparison with True is redundant for a real Boolean value, because True == True evaluates to True and False == True evaluates to False, so the result equals the value itself. For other values the comparison changes the meaning, as in the example above. The plain form lets Python apply the rule of truthiness (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The recommendation concerns conditions, not every use of a Boolean value: a program may still store, print and pass on True and False. If a program really must know that a value is exactly True and not merely true, it has to say so in its own words, and the reader should be told why.

nodes.example: if greeting: rather than if greeting == True:
nodes.definition: PEP 8 advises testing a Boolean directly instead of comparing it to True or False with ==.

nodes.label: Singleton comparison
nodes.body: The style guide says that comparisons to singletons like None should always be done with is or is not, never the equality operators (Van Rossum et al., 2001). The reference documentation repeats the advice when it describes None as a singleton (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: The style guide says that comparisons to singletons like None should always be done with is or is not, never the equality operators (Van Rossum et al., 2001). The reference documentation repeats the advice when it describes None as a singleton (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The reason lies in how the operators work. Equality can be customised by the kind of object that is compared, whereas the behaviour of is cannot be customised and it never raises an exception (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Asking whether a value is the one and only None is a question of identity, and the identity operator answers exactly that.

The test appears wherever a variable may hold the absence of a value, for example before a result is used. PEP 8 also gives the preferred spelling of the negative test: if foo is not None: is correct and if not foo is None: is wrong, because the two forms are equivalent but the first is more readable (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

With x = None, the expressions x is None and x is not None evaluate to True and False. The test asks only whether the value is the object None, and it does not look at the truth of the value: with x = [], x is not None evaluates to True although bool(x) is False.

PEP 8 warns against writing if x when the intention is if x is not None. The variable might have been set to some other value that counts as false, such as an empty container, and the shorter test would treat it as unset (Van Rossum et al., 2001). Choose between the plain truth test and the test against None according to the question that the program is really asking.

nodes.example: x is None rather than x == None
nodes.definition: PEP 8 asks that comparisons with singletons such as None use is or is not, never the equality operators.

nodes.label: Emptiness test
nodes.body: PEP 8 advises that, for sequences such as strings, lists and tuples, the program should use the fact that empty sequences are false. Its example shows if not seq: and if seq: as correct and if len(seq): and if not len(seq): as wrong (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

paras.text: PEP 8 advises that, for sequences such as strings, lists and tuples, the program should use the fact that empty sequences are false. Its example shows if not seq: and if seq: as correct and if len(seq): and if not len(seq): as wrong (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

The plain test says what is meant: does the sequence have content. It also works for every kind of sequence without asking for its length, and it reads like the English sentence it stands for. Python itself defines the truth of a sequence in this way, so the shorter test is not a trick but the documented rule (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The test appears when a program has collected something and must decide whether there is anything to process, for example whether the user typed a name or a search found results. The rule applies equally to strings, lists and tuples.

The documentation lists the empty string, the empty tuple and the empty list among the values that are considered false (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The two forms of the test therefore agree: bool([]) evaluates to False and len([]) evaluates to 0, and bool([1, 2]) evaluates to True and len([1, 2]) evaluates to 2.

The truth test cannot distinguish an empty sequence from the value None, since both are false. When the difference matters, test for None separately with is, as the section on singleton comparison explains. Remember also that the rule is about emptiness: a string that holds a space, or a list that holds a zero, is not empty.

nodes.example: if seq: rather than if len(seq):
nodes.definition: PEP 8 says to use the fact that empty sequences are false instead of testing their length.

nodes.label: Indentation style
nodes.body: The style guide's rules about indentation are short. It says to use four spaces per indentation level, that spaces are the preferred indentation method, that tabs should be used solely to remain consistent with code that is already indented with tabs, and that Python disallows mixing tabs and spaces for indentation (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

paras.text: The style guide's rules about indentation are short. It says to use four spaces per indentation level, that spaces are the preferred indentation method, that tabs should be used solely to remain consistent with code that is already indented with tabs, and that Python disallows mixing tabs and spaces for indentation (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

Because Python reads indentation as structure, a consistent habit prevents a whole class of errors that come from lines that look aligned but are not. Four spaces are wide enough to show the structure at a glance, and programmers who follow the same rule find each other's code familiar.
The convention holds for the examples of this chapter: the textbook indents the block of each if, elif and else clause by four spaces (Sweigart, 2025).

A line that is indented by one level more than the line above it opens a block, and a line that is indented by one level less closes one. The style guide also discourages compound statements, which put several statements on one line: if foo == 'blah': do_blah_thing() is called wrong, and the same is said for an else clause that is written on the same line as its suite (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

Python accepts other amounts of indentation than four, and it only insists that they are used consistently. A program that happens to run is therefore not necessarily a program in good style. Mixing tabs and spaces is the one choice that the language itself may refuse to read.

nodes.definition: PEP 8 asks for four spaces per level, spaces rather than tabs, and one statement per line.

nodes.label: Worked program
nodes.body: A worked program is a complete short program in which the ideas of a chapter are used together. Chapter 2 ends with two of them. Opposite Day uses if and else statements to set a Boolean variable and to reverse it, and the Dishonest Capacity Calculator uses an if and an elif clause to choose a conversion factor according to the unit that the user types (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A worked program is a complete short program in which the ideas of a chapter are used together. Chapter 2 ends with two of them. Opposite Day uses if and else statements to set a Boolean variable and to reverse it, and the Dishonest Capacity Calculator uses an if and an elif clause to choose a conversion factor according to the unit that the user types (Sweigart, 2025).

Isolated examples show one idea at a time, whereas a program shows how the ideas depend on each other: a comparison feeds a condition, the condition selects a block, the block assigns a variable and a later line uses it. Reading complete programs is the skill that the chapter has been preparing, and the second program also shows a typical bug that grows out of a missing branch.

The programs are saved as oppositeday.py and dishonestcapacity.py in the textbook, and they are the last examples before the summary and the practice questions (Sweigart, 2025). The first is a puzzle in logic, the second a small useful calculation.

The branch has one sub-branch, decision patterns, which pulls four patterns out of the programs: toggling a Boolean variable, accepting two spellings of one answer, noticing that a variable may never have been assigned, and guarding against input that no branch accepts.

The textbook is frank about the quality of its programs. It remarks that the Opposite Day program could be replaced by a single print and that the capacity program fails for an invalid unit (Sweigart, 2025). The programs are teaching devices, and learners should read them critically.

nodes.label: Decision pattern
nodes.body: A decision pattern is a way of using the flow control statements that recurs in many programs. The two worked programs of the textbook (Sweigart, 2025) contain four: the toggle, which reverses a Boolean variable; the case-insensitive test, which accepts several spellings of one answer; the unassigned name, which is a bug that appears when no branch runs; and the input guard, which is the cure for that bug.

paras.text: A decision pattern is a way of using the flow control statements that recurs in many programs. The two worked programs of the textbook (Sweigart, 2025) contain four: the toggle, which reverses a Boolean variable; the case-insensitive test, which accepts several spellings of one answer; the unassigned name, which is a bug that appears when no branch runs; and the input guard, which is the cure for that bug.

Patterns turn single statements into reusable solutions. A programmer who has seen the toggle once recognises it in every later program, and one who has seen the unassigned name once checks every chain of conditions for a missing else clause.

The section on each pattern takes the textbook's program as its example and checks its output by running it. The first two patterns are things to do, and the last two belong together as a problem and its remedy.

The last two patterns are a fault and its cure, and the fault can be produced on demand. A chain of if and elif clauses with no else leaves its variable unbound whenever no condition holds, so the next line stops the program with NameError: name 'answer' is not defined (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The input guard is the cure: a final else clause, or a loop that asks again, so that every path through the chain binds the name. The toggle needs only one line by comparison, since spam = not spam reverses a Boolean in place.

nodes.label: Toggle
nodes.body: To toggle a Boolean variable is to set it to its opposite Boolean value (Sweigart, 2025). In Python the idiom assigns the negation of the variable to the variable itself: flag = not flag. The textbook uses it in the Opposite Day program, where the line say_it_is_opposite_day = not say_it_is_opposite_day reverses the answer when today is Opposite Day.

paras.text: To toggle a Boolean variable is to set it to its opposite Boolean value (Sweigart, 2025). In Python the idiom assigns the negation of the variable to the variable itself: flag = not flag. The textbook uses it in the Opposite Day program, where the line say_it_is_opposite_day = not say_it_is_opposite_day reverses the answer when today is Opposite Day.

Many programs keep a switch that is on or off: a light, a mode, a player whose turn it is. The toggle changes such a switch without asking what its present state is, which makes the code shorter and removes one decision.

The Opposite Day program of the textbook has three if statements. The first sets say_it_is_opposite_day to True when today_is_opposite_day is True and to False otherwise. The second toggles the variable if today is Opposite Day. The third prints a message according to the variable (Sweigart, 2025).

With today_is_opposite_day set to True, the first statement sets the other variable to True, the second reverses it to False, and the third prints Today is not Opposite Day. With the first line changed to False, the first statement sets the variable to False, the second is skipped, and the program prints the same message (Sweigart, 2025). A short test shows the idiom: with flag = True, the line flag = not flag leaves False in flag.

The textbook points out that the program can never print Today is Opposite Day, whatever value the first variable has, and that the whole program could be replaced by one print statement (Sweigart, 2025). A sequence of decisions can cancel itself out, and the way to find out is to follow every path, as a flowchart does. The conditions of the program also compare a Boolean value with True, which the style guide advises against.

nodes.definition: Toggling sets a Boolean variable to its opposite value with not.

nodes.label: Case-insensitive test
nodes.body: A case-insensitive test is a condition that accepts an answer whether it is typed in uppercase or in lowercase. The textbook builds it from the Boolean operator or: the if and elif statements of the Dishonest Capacity Calculator use or so that the program works no matter whether the user enters the unit in lowercase or uppercase (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A case-insensitive test is a condition that accepts an answer whether it is typed in uppercase or in lowercase. The textbook builds it from the Boolean operator or: the if and elif statements of the Dishonest Capacity Calculator use or so that the program works no matter whether the user enters the unit in lowercase or uppercase (Sweigart, 2025).

Users type the same answer in different ways, and a program that accepts only one of them seems broken to everyone else. A test that covers both spellings costs one more comparison and saves the user an error message.

The program asks for the unit in which a drive is advertised and tests unit == 'TB' or unit == 'tb' and then unit == 'GB' or unit == 'gb'. For the first branch it computes the factor 1000000000000 / 1099511627776, which evaluates to 0.9094947017729282, and for the second 1000000000 / 1073741824, which evaluates to 0.9313225746154785 (Sweigart, 2025).

Each side of the or is a complete comparison, and the whole condition is true if either comparison is. For an advertised capacity of 10 TB the real capacity is 10 multiplied by the factor, which is 9.094947017729282, and round(9.094947017729282, 2) gives 9.09. The function str turns that number into the text '9.09', so that it can be joined to the message with a plus sign (Sweigart, 2025).

The test lists the accepted spellings and no others. A user who types Tb, with a capital T and a lowercase b, matches neither comparison, so 'Tb' == 'TB' or 'Tb' == 'tb' evaluates to False and no branch runs. Writing each spelling as a full comparison is also necessary, since unit == 'TB' or 'tb' is true for every unit.

nodes.definition: Two comparisons joined by or make a test accept either spelling of an answer.

nodes.label: Unassigned name
nodes.body: An unassigned name is a variable that the program uses without any assignment to it having been executed. In the Dishonest Capacity Calculator the variable discrepancy is assigned inside the if clause and the elif clause only. If the user enters a unit that is neither TB, tb, GB nor gb, neither clause runs and the variable is never created (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: An unassigned name is a variable that the program uses without any assignment to it having been executed. In the Dishonest Capacity Calculator the variable discrepancy is assigned inside the if clause and the elif clause only. If the user enters a unit that is neither TB, tb, GB nor gb, neither clause runs and the variable is never created (Sweigart, 2025).

The bug is typical of decisions without an alternative. The program does not fail at the decision, where the cause lies, but later at a line that uses the variable, and by then the connection to the decision is hard to see. The textbook notes that the user would not know that anything was wrong until Python tried to use the nonexistent variable (Sweigart, 2025).

Any chain of if and elif clauses that assigns a variable in each of its blocks, and has no else clause, can leave the variable unassigned. The situation is common when the program reads input, because the user can type anything.

When the program reaches the line that uses the variable, Python looks for the name, does not find it, and raises a NameError with the message name 'discrepancy' is not defined. The textbook says that the error points to the line where real_capacity is assigned, which is the line that first uses the variable, although the true origin lies in the decision (Sweigart, 2025).

The remedy is to make sure that the variable always receives a value, or that the program stops when it cannot. The next section shows the second approach with an else clause. A third approach, which is not used in the textbook, is to give the variable a first value before the chain begins.

nodes.definition: A variable that is assigned only inside the branches of a chain does not exist when no branch runs, and using it raises a NameError.

nodes.label: Input guard
nodes.body: An input guard is a branch that deals with input which none of the expected cases accept. The textbook identifies the true origin of the unassigned variable as the fact that the program does not handle the case where the user enters an invalid unit, and says that the simplest remedy is an else clause that displays a message such as You must enter TB or GB and then calls the sys.exit() function to quit the program (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: An input guard is a branch that deals with input which none of the expected cases accept. The textbook identifies the true origin of the unassigned variable as the fact that the program does not handle the case where the user enters an invalid unit, and says that the simplest remedy is an else clause that displays a message such as You must enter TB or GB and then calls the sys.exit() function to quit the program (Sweigart, 2025).

A guard changes a confusing failure into a clear one. Instead of a NameError that mentions a variable the user has never heard of, the user is told what to type. For the programmer, the guard states in the code which inputs the program is prepared to handle, and the else clause is the natural place for all the others.

The function sys.exit belongs to the module sys, which a program imports with the statement import sys, as Chapter 1 explained for packages. The textbook defers a full description of the function to the next chapter (Sweigart, 2025).

The documentation says that sys.exit raises a SystemExit exception, signalling an intention to exit the interpreter. If it is given a string, the string is printed to the error output and the exit status, the number that a finished program hands back to the system, is 1, and the documentation calls sys.exit with an error message a quick way to exit a program when an error occurs (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the capacity program, with the unit 'KB', the else clause runs, the message You must enter TB or GB is shown and the program ends before the variable is used.

The guard must come last, after all the accepted cases, because else takes everything that is left. It also does not replace checking the number the user types: the textbook converts the advertised capacity with float, which would fail for text that is not a number. A guard handles the cases the programmer thought of, and thinking of them is the real work.

nodes.example: else: sys.exit('You must enter TB or GB')
nodes.definition: An else clause can reject input that no earlier branch accepts, report a message and end the program with sys.exit.

nodes.label: Error report
nodes.body: An error report is what Python prints when it cannot carry out a line of a program. The report names the kind of error and gives a message about it, and for errors that happen while the program runs it also shows the lines through which execution arrived. The chapter meets four kinds of error: SyntaxError, NameError, TypeError and ZeroDivisionError (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: An error report is what Python prints when it cannot carry out a line of a program. The report names the kind of error and gives a message about it, and for errors that happen while the program runs it also shows the lines through which execution arrived. The chapter meets four kinds of error: SyntaxError, NameError, TypeError and ZeroDivisionError (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Reading the report correctly is the first skill of debugging, the work of finding and removing the cause of a fault in a program. The tutorial notes that the last line of an error message indicates what happened and that the type of the exception is printed as part of the message (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A learner who reads that line, instead of looking only at the length of the report, finds the cause much faster.

The textbook shows error reports when it enters true, when it assigns to False, and when the capacity program uses an unassigned variable (Sweigart, 2025). The examples of this branch add the reports that a learner is likely to see while practising the chapter: a missing colon, a bad indentation, a comparison between a number and a string, and a division by zero.

The branch has one sub-branch, the kinds of error, with a section for each kind and one for the traceback, the report as a whole. Every message quoted in the branch was produced by running the line in question, because the wording of messages changes between releases.

The message wording is not a stable part of the language. Python 3.14 words some messages more helpfully than Python 3.12 does, as the section on the else clause showed for an elif that follows an else, so the kind of error is more reliable than its message.

nodes.label: Kind of error
nodes.body: A kind of error is the type that Python prints at the start of the last line of an error report. The tutorial distinguishes syntax errors, which the parser finds when it reads the text, from exceptions, which are errors detected during execution in a statement or expression that is syntactically correct (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The kinds seen in this chapter are SyntaxError, with its subclass IndentationError, NameError, TypeError and ZeroDivisionError.

paras.text: A kind of error is the type that Python prints at the start of the last line of an error report. The tutorial distinguishes syntax errors, which the parser finds when it reads the text, from exceptions, which are errors detected during execution in a statement or expression that is syntactically correct (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The kinds seen in this chapter are SyntaxError, with its subclass IndentationError, NameError, TypeError and ZeroDivisionError.

Each kind points to a different class of cause. A SyntaxError says that the text of the program is wrong, a NameError that a name has no value, a TypeError that an operation was applied to values of the wrong types, and a ZeroDivisionError that a number was divided by zero. Knowing the family narrows the search before the message has been read.

The sections of this branch define each kind with the wording of the documentation, show a line from the chapter that produces it and report the message that the line really produces. The section on the traceback then explains the report as a whole.

The report names the kind on its last line, and every kind in this chapter can be produced in a single line. The expression 1 / 0 raises ZeroDivisionError: division by zero, joining a string to a number raises a TypeError saying that only a str may be concatenated to a str, reading a name before any assignment raises NameError: name 'spam' is not defined, and a header such as if spam = 42: is refused before the program starts with a SyntaxError (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
