Reading the kind first and the message second is the shortest route from the report to the cause.

nodes.label: Exception
nodes.body: An exception is an error that is detected while a program runs. The tutorial explains that even if a statement or expression is syntactically correct, it may cause an error when an attempt is made to execute it, and that errors detected during execution are called exceptions and are not unconditionally fatal (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A program can be written to handle an exception, a topic that comes later in the course; most exceptions are not handled and result in an error report.

paras.text: An exception is an error that is detected while a program runs. The tutorial explains that even if a statement or expression is syntactically correct, it may cause an error when an attempt is made to execute it, and that errors detected during execution are called exceptions and are not unconditionally fatal (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A program can be written to handle an exception, a topic that comes later in the course; most exceptions are not handled and result in an error report.

The word separates two moments at which a line can fail. A syntax error is found when the program text is read, before anything runs, whereas an exception arises only when execution reaches the line. This explains why a faulty line inside a block that is skipped does not disturb a program that never executes it.

The NameError, TypeError and ZeroDivisionError of this chapter are exceptions, and so is the SystemExit that the function sys.exit raises. Each report names the exception: the tutorial's examples show ZeroDivisionError, NameError and TypeError, and the type printed is the name of the built-in exception that occurred (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

When an exception is raised, Python stops the statement that raised it, looks for code that handles it, and prints the error report if none is found. The last line of the report gives the exception's type and the rest of the line gives details that depend on the type and the cause (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The built-in exception names are ordinary built-in names and not reserved keywords (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

An exception is not a syntax error and cannot be found by reading the text alone. The same line can run in one execution and raise an exception in another, depending on the data. The exception SystemExit is a special case: it is raised on purpose to end the program, and the interpreter then exits without printing a traceback (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.example: an error detected while a program runs
nodes.definition: An exception is an error detected when a statement or expression is executed; unless the program handles it, the program stops with an error report.

nodes.label: SyntaxError
nodes.body: A SyntaxError is raised when the parser, the part of Python that reads the text of a program, encounters a syntax error, that is, text that does not follow the grammar, the set of rules that say how correct Python text is written (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The tutorial calls such errors parsing errors and says that they are perhaps the most common kind of complaint while one is still learning the language. An IndentationError is a subclass of SyntaxError (a kind of error defined as a more specific case of another kind) for errors in the indentation, and a TabError is a subclass of that for the inconsistent use of tabs and spaces (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A SyntaxError is raised when the parser, the part of Python that reads the text of a program, encounters a syntax error, that is, text that does not follow the grammar, the set of rules that say how correct Python text is written (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The tutorial calls such errors parsing errors and says that they are perhaps the most common kind of complaint while one is still learning the language. An IndentationError is a subclass of SyntaxError (a kind of error defined as a more specific case of another kind) for errors in the indentation, and a TabError is a subclass of that for the inconsistent use of tabs and spaces (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Because the parser reads the whole text of a program before anything runs, a SyntaxError stops the program at once, and none of it is executed. It is the first kind of error that a learner meets, and it is also the kind whose report is the most helpful: it shows the offending line and arrows that point to the place where the error was detected.

The chapter's examples produce it in several ways. The line False = 2 + 2 gives cannot assign to False; the line if = 3 gives invalid syntax; the header if True without its colon gives expected ':'; and the condition of an if statement written with a single equals sign gives a message that suggests ==. An else clause with a condition gives invalid syntax.

The parser reports the place where it noticed the problem. The tutorial adds that this is not always the place that needs to be fixed: in its example the error is detected at the function print, because a colon is missing just before it (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A missing colon, a missing quotation mark or a wrong operator are the most frequent causes.

Do not stop at the first message. When the reported line looks correct, look at the lines before it, because an unclosed bracket is often noticed only at a later line. The wording of the message differs between versions of Python: an elif written after an else clause is reported in Python 3.14 as 'elif' block follows an 'else' block, and in Python 3.12 only as invalid syntax.

nodes.definition: A SyntaxError means that the text of the program is not valid Python; an IndentationError is a kind of SyntaxError.

nodes.label: NameError
nodes.body: A NameError is raised when a local or global name is not found. The documentation adds that the associated value is an error message that includes the name that could not be found (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The message therefore always has the same shape: name, followed by the missing name in quotation marks, followed by is not defined.

paras.text: A NameError is raised when a local or global name is not found. The documentation adds that the associated value is an error message that includes the name that could not be found (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The message therefore always has the same shape: name, followed by the missing name in quotation marks, followed by is not defined.

A name in Python exists only after it has been assigned, so any use of a name before its assignment, or of a name that was spelled differently, fails in this way. The error is therefore a precise report about the program: it names the exact word that Python could not find.

The textbook produces it in the interactive shell by entering true in lowercase, which gives name 'true' is not defined (Sweigart, 2025). The tutorial produces it with 4 + spam*3 when spam has no value (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the capacity program the name discrepancy is missing when the unit is invalid.

When Python meets a name in an expression, it looks for a value that was assigned to that name. If none exists, it raises the error at once, even if a similar name does exist, and it does not substitute the similar name. The printed report of the releases used for this chapter does add a hint after the message: for true it ends with Did you mean: 'True'?, while the message of the error itself stays name 'true' is not defined. A name is case sensitive, so true and True are different words, and a name that is assigned only inside a block that did not run is also missing.

The error is reported where the name is used, not where it should have been assigned. When the cause is a typing mistake the fix is local, but when the name was assigned only inside a branch that did not run, as with discrepancy, the cause is in the logic and the fix is a new branch or a first value.

nodes.definition: A NameError means that a name was used that has no value in the program: it was never assigned, or it is misspelled.

nodes.label: TypeError
nodes.body: A TypeError is raised when an operation or function is applied to an object of inappropriate type. The associated value is a string giving details about the type mismatch (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It is the error of Chapter 1, where a string and a number were added, and it returns in this chapter when an order comparison is applied to unrelated types.

paras.text: A TypeError is raised when an operation or function is applied to an object of inappropriate type. The associated value is a string giving details about the type mismatch (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It is the error of Chapter 1, where a string and a number were added, and it returns in this chapter when an order comparison is applied to unrelated types.

The error protects against silent guessing. Python could try to convert the string '4' to a number or the number 3 to a string, but either choice would hide a mistake. The language refuses and reports both types that were involved, which is the information needed to repair the line.

In this chapter it appears when a number is compared by order with text, as in 3 < '4', which raises a TypeError with the message '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'str'. The comparison for equality never raises it, since values of different types are simply unequal.

The operator < looks at the types of its two operands. For an integer and a string there is no defined order, so Python stops. The reference documentation confirms that the ordering operators are only defined where they make sense (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The message names the operator and the type of each operand.

A TypeError usually means that a conversion is missing. A value that was typed in with input is a string even if it looks like a number, so it must be converted with int or float before it is compared by order with a number. The reverse repair, comparing both as text, is possible but gives the code-point ordering that the section on string ordering described.

nodes.definition: A TypeError means that an operation was applied to a value of a type that does not support it.

error.out: TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'str'

nodes.label: ZeroDivisionError
nodes.body: A ZeroDivisionError is raised when the second argument of a division or modulo operation (the remainder of a division) is zero. The documentation adds that the associated value is a string indicating the type of the operands and the operation (Python Software Foundation, 2026). For the expression 1 / 0 the message is division by zero.

paras.text: A ZeroDivisionError is raised when the second argument of a division or modulo operation (the remainder of a division) is zero. The documentation adds that the associated value is a string indicating the type of the operands and the operation (Python Software Foundation, 2026). For the expression 1 / 0 the message is division by zero.

Division by zero has no answer, so Python stops the program and says so. The error often appears at the end of a chain of calculations, and the cause lies earlier, in a value that should not have been zero.

The tutorial's first example of an exception is the line 10 * (1/0) (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In this chapter the error is the thing that short-circuit evaluation can avoid: the guard x != 0 and 10 / x > 2 never divides when x is zero, and the expression 1 or 1 / 0 never reaches its division.

Python evaluates the operands, sees the zero, and raises the error before it produces a result. The remainder operator behaves in the same way, so 1 % 0 raises a ZeroDivisionError too; its message is division by zero in Python 3.14 and integer modulo by zero in Python 3.12. A division in a branch that does not run is not evaluated, so it cannot raise the error.

The error is not prevented by testing the result, because there is none. The test has to be made on the divisor before the division is carried out, which is what a guarding condition does. Division of a float by 0.0 raises the same error: 1 / 0.0 gives the message division by zero in Python 3.14 and float division by zero in Python 3.12.

nodes.definition: A ZeroDivisionError means that a division or remainder operation had zero as its second operand.

nodes.label: Traceback
nodes.body: A traceback is the report that Python prints when an error stops a program. The tutorial explains that the last line of the report indicates what happened, that the rest of that line gives details based on the kind of error, and that the preceding part shows the context where the exception occurred, in the form of a list of the lines of source code through which the program reached the error (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A traceback is the report that Python prints when an error stops a program. The tutorial explains that the last line of the report indicates what happened, that the rest of that line gives details based on the kind of error, and that the preceding part shows the context where the exception occurred, in the form of a list of the lines of source code through which the program reached the error (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The traceback is a map from the symptom to the place. The last line says what went wrong, and the lines above it say where, so that a programmer can go straight to the line that raised the error and to the chain of lines that led to it. The textbook shows the shape of the report in its first examples (Sweigart, 2025).

A traceback appears in the interactive shell after a failed line, and in the output of a program saved in a file when it stops. The capacity program, run with a unit that no branch accepts and without a guard, ends with a traceback whose first line is Traceback (most recent call last): and whose last line is NameError: name 'discrepancy' is not defined.

The report begins with the line Traceback (most recent call last): and then lists the position in the file, the line number and the source line in which the error arose. Because the most recent call is last, the final entry is the nearest to the cause, and the closing line names the kind of error and its message.

A traceback is printed only when an error is not handled. A program that stops with sys.exit and a message prints the message and no traceback, because the interpreter treats SystemExit as a request to leave and, when it is not handled, exits without printing a traceback (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Read the traceback from the bottom: the last line names the error, and the line above it shows the code that raised it.

nodes.definition: A traceback is the report that Python prints for an uncaught error: the lines through which execution reached the failure, and last the kind and message of the error.

stories.title: The man inside the bool type
stories.who: George Boole, self-taught mathematician, first professor of mathematics at Cork
stories.where: Lincoln, England and Queen's College, Cork
stories.story: A shoemaker's son from Lincoln taught himself mathematics, and in 'The Mathematical Analysis of Logic' (1847) and 'The Laws of Thought' (1854) showed that reasoning itself obeys algebra: statements as values, AND and OR as operations. He never saw a computer. A century later his algebra became the switching logic of every circuit, and Python names its True-and-False type bool after him - every condition on today's slides is Boole's arithmetic.
stories.lesson: Every if statement runs on one Victorian's algebra
stories.source: George Boole, 'The Mathematical Analysis of Logic' (1847) and 'An Investigation of the Laws of Thought' (1854); biography at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Boole. Portrait: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stories.title: The whitespace that is the syntax
stories.who: Guido van Rossum, carrying a lesson from the ABC language at CWI
stories.where: documented in Python's own design FAQ
stories.story: Most languages mark blocks with braces and treat indentation as decoration; Python makes the indentation itself the block. The choice came from ABC, the teaching language Guido van Rossum worked on at CWI before Python, and the design FAQ still defends it: what you see is what the interpreter sees, so a program cannot look right and group wrong. The chapter's two indentation programs run the same lines indented two ways - and print different stories.
stories.lesson: In Python the layout cannot lie about the logic
stories.source: The Python design FAQ, 'Why does Python use indentation for grouping of statements?' (docs.python.org/3/faq/design.html); the ABC lineage per van Rossum's documented history of the language.

stories.title: A thirty-year-old wish, granted in 3.10
stories.who: PEPs 634-636 by Brandt Bucher, Guido van Rossum and colleagues
stories.story: For decades Python answered 'where is my switch statement?' with dictionaries and elif chains. In February 2021 the Steering Council accepted structural pattern matching - PEPs 634, 635 and 636 - and Python 3.10 shipped the match statement that October. It is more than a switch: patterns destructure data and bind names. The chapter's match programs - command words, status codes, captures, guards - run the real thing, and their transcripts are on these slides.

ndiag.title: How execution runs through a chain of if, elif and else
ndiag.read_from: chapter 2, the Branching section: If statement (its block executes when the condition is True and is skipped when it is False), Elif clause (another condition, checked only if all of the previous conditions were False), Else clause (executed only when the condition of the if statement is False; it has no condition), Branch chain (exactly one if statement, any elif clauses after it, and else to be sure that at least one clause is executed)
ndiag.why: the explanations describe what execution does in order - evaluate the if condition, run or skip the block, check the next elif condition only when the earlier ones were False, fall to else when nothing else has run - which is a procedure with decisions: a workflow

Is the condition of the if statement True?
Execute the indented block of the if clause
Evaluate the condition of the elif clause
Execute the indented block of the elif clause
Does the chain end with an else clause?
Execute the else clause: it has no condition
Skip every block: no clause of the chain is executed
Execution continues with the statement after the chain

ndiag.title: How a match statement chooses a case block
ndiag.read_from: chapter 2, the Pattern matching section: Match statement (takes an expression and compares its value with successive patterns given as case blocks; only the first pattern that matches is executed; if no case matches, none of the branches runs), Case pattern (matched against the subject value; the outcome is a success or a failure and possibly the binding of matched values to names), Guard (if followed by an expression; it must succeed for the code inside the case block to execute), Wildcard pattern (the underscore always succeeds and binds no name)
ndiag.why: the explanations describe a procedure in order - evaluate the subject, try each case pattern in turn, check its guard, run the first case block whose pattern and guard succeed, or run nothing - with decisions at every case: a workflow
